The theory and the associated experiments provide a framework for optimizing the training of deep neural network layers in a manner that is both physiologically inspired and mathematically sound. ACN protocol integrates Decentralized Power Control (DFPC) method, where users adapt their transmission powers autonomously in response to changing conditions, and enables the base station to adjust subcarriers and modulation schemes adaptively based on real-time information. A comprehensive system performance assessment is provided by modeling the DFPC process and analyzing the modified log-normal distribution of system sum rate. The proposed protocol is compatible with 5G standards and can be applied to other OFDMA-based systems with similar characteristics. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells allocate uplink and downlink time slots based on observed traffic conditions, effectively modeling a model allocation problem. Our analysis reveals that in general, TDD systems experience increased interference at cell boundaries, a phenomenon we quantify as the "interference disparity." This strategy involves allocated cells switching from uplink to downlink modes if they have sufficiently low traffic loads. Through numerical experiments using real NYC taxi data, our results show a notable increase in system throughput by implementing this policy, resulting in a 25% better performance under certain traffic conditions. In some scenarios, our proposed approach achieves a 40% better performance compared to traditional fixed TDD systems. Our research centered on developing a novel neural network called the Hamiltonian Gradient Neural Network (HGNN), which enables the computation of gradients via Hamiltonian Optimization. Leveraging the advantages of both mini-batch stochastic gradient descent and HMC, we derived the Hamiltonian Gradient Neural Network by incorporating the mini-batch HMC computation of gradients into the general framework of deep neural networks. Our model's performance was evaluated across multiple datasets, revealing improved accuracy and reduced overfitting when using the Hamiltonian Gradient Neural Network in place of the conventional backpropagation. The HGNN employs both Hamiltonian Optimization and the Monte Carlo estimation of gradients in parallel, resulting in which the Hamiltonian Gradient Neural Network can also be viewed as an example of a dual update method deep neural network. Furthermore, our research indicates that the Hamiltonian Gradient Neural Network achieves these performance gains at a comparable computational cost to standard deep neural networks. Machine learning models are utilized in various applications to make predictions and classifications, however, their effectiveness is short-lived due to their lack of inherent common sense and inability to comprehend the context of emerging situations. As these models degrade over time, particularly after they have been deployed, their performance suffers significantly from the accumulation of inaccuracies. As a result, their classification outputs often change frequently, leading to trust being lost in the model's ability to classify correctly. This research proposes an innovative multi-agent framework that is scalable, flexible, and capable of refining machine learning models in real-time by incorporating their reliability into their learning process. A rating system based on trust is introduced, where it assigns a level of reliability to the model's classification outputs, which in turn activates a learning loop to focus on correcting its most uncertain and least reliable predictions. This data enrichment process is carried out through a selective approach, where only the model's most certain and reliable predictions are used as constraints while allowing it to freely classify the more uncertain and unreliable predictions. This results in refined models that are not only more accurate but also more consistent in their outputs, thus enhancing their performance and level of trustworthiness. This multi-agent system is robust, adaptable, and efficient as it incorporates a variety of advanced artificial intelligence techniques, such as deep learning, optimization methods, and preference learning. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through a real-world application involving the classification of seismic activities, where it shows that it is possible to maintain a high level of accuracy while reducing the degree of classification variability by over 20% and the reliability gap by over 15% in a scenario where the dataset is modified to include more uncertainties. This research provides a novel solution to the persistent inaccuracy issue that affects machine learning models after they have been deployed, and it has the potential to be applied to a variety of domains and scenarios. Additionally, this paper includes an exhaustive overview of the methods that have been proposed to address the long-standing challenges of maintaining the accuracy and reliability of machine learning models after they have been deployed, and a comprehensive analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of all the different techniques that have been proposed over the years. This innovation follows from a thorough analysis of the twisted Hecke algebra itself, inspired by the Volume Hypothesis. Our findings also create connections between our quantum invariant, the colored Jones polynomials, and an extended version of the Witten-Reshetikhin-Turaev invariants, all while considering various values of the volume parameter. These relationships hold under constraints specified by the Volume Hypothesis, and our approach allows for the introduction of a new Casimir function within the topological Chern-Simons theory. This construction allows for the incorporation of the volume parameter into the Chern-Simons theory itself, and thus provides a way to relate our quantum invariant to the refined version of the Witten invariants. This connection is made with the constraint that the volume parameter is linked to the Chern-Simons level, and is therefore an integer in this context. Our results also imply an extension of the colored Jones polynomials, and we outline how this could be further related to the refined topological invariants through the use of a scaling function, as previously proposed. However, it is essential to note that this proposal necessitates the verification of the Quantum Volume Conjecture. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Our proposed method, Context-gloss Enhancement for Word Sense Disambiguation (CGE-WSD), aims to resolve this issue by utilizing and generating contextual information.  Our context-gloss model is centered on two main components: a context generation module and a gloss generation module.  For both tasks, we utilize a state-of-the-art language model with a masked language model objective, where words are replaced with [MASK] to be filled by the model's output based on the context provided by the training data.  Our model's ability is evaluated using the SenseVal dataset, and the results show an improvement of 8% in the WSD task's overall score when compared to a baseline model.  Furthermore, our model's ability to generate high-quality glosses is verified through human annotations.  Our code is available for public access on GitHub at the specified URL. To detect the top quark generation, our research considers proton-nucleus collisions at the LHC, specifically looking for the production of top and bottom quarks in forward rapidity. We examine the characteristics of the quark masses and the relevant mixing angle to determine the signature of the top quark generation in its production. In the case where the W boson's mass is ignored, we find the cross section for top quark production to be influenced by the mixing angle in proportion to $\sin^2(2\theta)^2$. Furthermore, we identify the minimum visible $p_T$ for the leading top or bottom quark to be around $200$ GeV, making its detection via quarkonium via $g \to \bar{t} \bar{t}$ or $g \to \bar{b} \bar{b}$ two-to-two hard to achieve. However, detecting the top quark generation through quarkonium via $q \bar{q} \to \gamma, \text{Z} + \text{invisible}$ in proton-nucleus collisions at the LHC is feasible with a required integrated luminosity of $10$ fb$^{-1}$. A two-dimensional mass correlation between the top and bottom quarks can aid in identifying their generation through a combination of kinematic and dynamic relationships in $t \bar{t}$ production. Furthermore, the influence of the irrelevance of the W boson's mass can be mitigated by exploring the characteristics of the quark masses and the relevant mixing angle. A detailed analysis using a purpose-built simulator for proton-nucleus collisions at the LHC demonstrates the feasibility of detecting the top quark generation through quarkonium in colliding beams. In addition to the signature in $t \bar{t}$ production, our research also finds the existence of the top quark generation in $t \bar{s}$ and $s \bar{t}$ production and identifies the most prominent signature in $t \bar{t}$ production as involving top and bottom quarks in forward rapidity. To illustrate the significance of confidentiality for graph data, we can consider how attack vectors like social engineering capitalize on the intricate connections present in these datasets. To effectively safeguard sensitive information within these systems, the practice of secure multi-party computation has become indispensable. A key issue here is modeling context from both local (activity context) and overall (dataset context) video content. It has been observed that existing methods typically focus on capturing local context but overlook the importance of understanding the ordering of activities within a dataset. In contrast, modeling just the order of activities within a dataset does not guarantee a comprehensive understanding of the context. To tackle this problem, we propose Context-Aware Linear Descriptive Factors (CALDF) for the dual context consolidation of local and global video context. Our method starts with a linear factorization of training videos to derive a reduced set of descriptive factors that capture the order of activities in the dataset. By incorporating these factors, we obtain a more refined representation of video data and enhance the learning of activity codes through a two-path approach. Our model is then used for activity coding and recognition. Extensive experiments on widely-used datasets (e.g. TARTANTRA, 3DLabeledMIMIC, and PAVIOUS) demonstrate the superiority of our approach over the state-of-the-art methods. The concept known as "Palm Tree Mode" in modern tokamaks is not clearly understood and its connection to ELMs needs further clarification. Our work suggests breaking down ELMs into two categories: Type Elms, following the classic impact-recycling model, and Double Peaking Structures, which share similarities with the "Palm Tree Mode" and may arise from a different causal mechanism involving a different class of coherent modes. We propose that DSTs have an independent root cause and may provide a means to enhance pedestal understanding. Discovering vulnerabilities in modern software via fuzzing has become increasingly difficult due to various obstacles caused by the complex interplay between software components and diverse input data.  Despite the challenges, fuzzers have achieved notable success in identifying vulnerabilities in recent years.  One factor contributing to their effectiveness is the widespread sharing of vulnerability discovery information, which includes insights gained from the testing process itself, the software's behavior under stress, and the input data used to trigger vulnerabilities.  However, there are sections of the software development community that are critical of the approach taken by those sharing such information, as it does not consider the underlying source code, but rather focuses solely on the software's external behavior.  Interestingly, research has shown that analyzing the software's external behavior offers a richer source of information than an examination of its internal code.  Furthermore, because the vast majority of software vulnerabilities arise from errors in its external manifestation rather than its source code, fuzzers that rely on this approach are often more efficient in their testing, as they are able to cover a greater portion of the software's external surface with the same amount of testing resources.  In light of these factors, the field of combined testing has been rebranded as "combinatorial testing" to better reflect the approach taken by those sharing their experiences and the underlying principles of source code analysis.  As a result of these changes, the focus has shifted from the source code to the software's external behavior, characterized by its combinatory properties, stress patterns, and input data structures.  Consequently, the community has adopted new metrics and methods for evaluating the effectiveness of fuzzers, stress testers, and combinatorial testers, as well as new taxonomic classifications and product line studies.  This combined testing approach has resulted in the discovery of more complex vulnerabilities, including multi-component vulnerabilities and situations in which the cause of the error cannot be deduced from the error message alone.  In recognition of these achievements, the term "combined testing" is now considered a synonym for the art of finding vulnerabilities in modern software via fuzzing.  As a result, the term "combinatorial testing" is no longer applicable, as it is now viewed as a historical reference to an earlier, less sophisticated approach to source code analysis.  Consequently, the name "Combined Testing" has been adopted as the official name for the annual combined testing conference, which has become a premier forum for the presentation of new research and the exchange of ideas among members of the combined testing community. One common technique used to study interactions between light and matter is single-beam absorption spectroscopy, and it has been applied to a variety of situations including gas phase, plasma environments, and cold atom assemblies. A key factor affecting the outcome of this method is the photon scattering effect, which can be significant when dealing with narrow absorption lines and large numbers of ground states. This effect has been thoroughly assessed in previous contexts; however, there is a lack of analytical models that account for the photon scattering in a single-beam absorption spectroscopy setup when measuring absorption lines with a depth of less than a decimal fraction of their maximum value. In our research, we developed a mathematical model to analyze this phenomenon and our findings match experimental results obtained with an ultracold strontium vapor. By varying key variables, our model also enabled us to create a practical approach for determining the density of atoms within the ground state and the scattering coefficient from the shape of absorption lines, even when they are weak. This has significant implications for applications involving ultracold atom systems, where the interaction between scattered photons can result in phenomena such as laser induced phase oscillations and the creation of entanglement. As a result, our research demonstrates that single beam absorption spectroscopy can serve as an effective method for investigating the properties of ultracold gases in a single beam absorption setup. Furthermore, our model highlights that in such systems, the photon scattering effect cannot be disregarded when interpreting the outcome of this technique. It is essential to acknowledge the contributions of three co-authors, A. Gilroy, J. D. Wright and S. L. Glaser, to this research. Their input was instrumental in furthering our comprehension of the phenomena underlying ultracold absorption spectroscopy. In fact, it was through discussions with one of these co-authors, Stephen Glaser, that our interest in this topic was initially sparked. His guidance and expertise proved invaluable in the development of our model. In the paper, our theoretical approach is complemented by the experimental results obtained by the University of Kansas research group led by J. D. Wright. Although our model is applicable to any species, we chose strontium atoms as the subject of our study due in part to the contributions of the University of Kansas research group and also because it is one of the most frequently used substances in quantum information processing experiments. As such, single-beam absorption spectroscopy offers a practical means for monitoring the state of these gases in real-time, a capability that is crucial for the effective execution of such experiments.

This sequence, as it accounts for respiratory fluctuations and patient movement, allows for the acquisition of clear cross-sectional images without the need for image registration or robust respiratory synchronization. To minimize disturbances from movement and respiration, in-vivo scans are performed at slower repetition rates. The introduction of extended acquisition times for multi-echo data enables more precise calculation of contrast images using a variety of weighting methods, including T2-weighted images. The technique was successfully applied to scan full bodies during free-breathing periods of up to 20 seconds in both healthy subjects and patients with cardiac conditions, producing high-quality 4D data available for further analysis and medical diagnosis. The innovative method presents a viable alternative to compressed sensing and sparse reconstruction techniques commonly used in accelerated 4D MRI scans. The sequence was further tested on larger animals, such as adults and one child, with positive results. Notably, for the Ising model on a honeycomb lattice, using this method we found the disorderized region to be more extensive than previously estimated based on exponent calculations. Additionally, our method can be adapted to investigate the effects of lattice geometry changes on the phase structure of lattice models. For example, modifying the diamond lattice to resemble a random tree lattice causes the system to shift from a disordered state to an ordered state. Our approach can also be applied to models involving non-compact lattice structures, such as the Ising model on a lattice that represents a complex network of paths. Graph neural networks, in particular those utilizing graph convolutional networks, have gained significant attention for their effective combination of node feature and structure information. GCNs can be highly efficient at various tasks such as node classification, visualization, and prediction, yet they can also be inherently opaque, complicating their integration into applications that require transparent decision-making processes. We have developed a novel approach called Lean-Sparse GCNs, which not only reduces unnecessary degrees of freedom but also learns a sparse and meaningful substructure representing the most critical graph connections. By combining this with a threshold-based neighbourhood, Lean-Sparse GCNs successfully balances the trade-off between model performance and understandability. Our experiments showcase Lean-Sparse GCNs' capability to create more accurate and interpretable models in comparison to conventional GCNs and other alternative models. Furthermore, our method is deemed practical for real-world applications due to its efficient training process. Lean-Sparse GCNs achieves comparable performance to conventional GCNs on benchmark datasets, with an average of 0.8% decrease in accuracy, while achieving a significant 85.7% reduction in edges in the learned substructure. Lean-Sparse GCNs' flexibility in edge selection allows it to create a diverse range of understandable models, from sparse subgraphs to overlapping local structures. Our method is highly adaptable to a variety of applications and datasets, such as classification, visualization, and prediction tasks, due to its flexible layer that can be easily integrated into a broad range of graph neural networks, such as graph attention networks and message passing neural networks. CountSketch can be seen as a form of collision-based sketching, where the significance of a vector entry is determined by the number of sketch matrix measurements it intersects, and has been extensively studied under the assumption of independent inputs. Research into the Effective Field Theories of a Standard Model Higgs boson is ongoing with the hope of distinguishing it from the Standard Model through experimentation. To understand the requirements for such experimentation to find differences, we have calculated the production of two Higgs bosons in the interaction of electron and positron in a collider, considering various possible interactions between Higgs bosons and other particles as reference points. These reference points include those derived from theories involving extra Higgs bosons, grand unified theories, and theories involving extra dimensions, and we have determined the minimum energy needed to produce two Higgs bosons clearly in a collider under different assumptions about the characteristics of the Higgs bosons and the nature of the effective theories. Furthermore, we have found that the responsiveness of the production of two Higgs bosons to its internal structure varies significantly with the nature of the interaction and that some interactions cause the production to result in two Higgs bosons at a much higher energy than others, and that the most sensitive way to distinguish the nature of the Higgs bosons is by observing the production of two Higgs bosons at energies below 500 TeV in a collider, and that the most important detectors to use for such a discovery are the b-tagging system, the forward proton taggers, and the detection of the decay of Higgs bosons into bosons. Additionally, we have found that the production of two Higgs bosons by exchanging a virtual Higgs boson, known as a resonance, at an energy below the threshold of producing two Higgs bosons at once, is also an important way to discover the unique characteristics of the Standard Model Higgs boson, and that the minimum energy needed to produce two Higgs bosons clearly in a collider by this method is around 10-20 TeV higher than the energy needed to produce two Higgs bosons at once, and that the most sensitive way to discover the unique characteristics of the Standard Model Higgs boson by this method is by observing the production of two Higgs bosons in a collider with an energy of around 1.1-1.3 TeV and a luminosity of around 10-100 times the current luminosity of the Large Hadron Collider. We investigated the motion of a cylindrical solid within a layer of granular material that is saturated with a fluid by taking high-speed video of the interaction and performing detailed force measurements as the cylinder is pulled across the surface. Depending on the angle at which the cylinder is positioned, its movement creates distinct patterns of erosion and the resulting force exerted on the cylinder varies significantly. This force difference is most pronounced when the cylinder is tilted by 90 degrees, resulting in an enhanced forward force of up to 75 times the weight of the cylinder compared to its backward force. A similar force disparity occurs when the cylinder is tilted by 0 and 180 degrees but is less notable. This asymmetry cannot be explained by factors such as friction or the shape of the cavity formed around the cylinder and is instead attributed to the unequal release of stress within the granular bed along different directions. A similar stress phenomenon occurs even when the cylinder is stationary, leading to a persistent "stick-slip" movement. This research provides new insights into the complex interactions within dry granular materials and could also be applied to better understand similar phenomena in fluid-filled environments. Complex high-dimensional physical processes often call for the use of multiple measurement functions to derive key variables, making interpretation and estimation of these processes challenging due to their inherent intricacy and the high degree of dimensionality, which is typically characterized as $\mathcal{O}(p\gg 1)$ for an $p$-dimensional parameter space. To address this issue, researchers have historically employed a variety of techniques such as dimensionality reduction methods in conjunction with Markov Chain Monte Carlo to some extent, but these approaches tend to be time-consuming and impractical for processes that involve costly system simulations to estimate the likelihood function. Furthermore, existing applications have demonstrated the feasibility of using a limited set of observable functions to derive the variables of interest, which in turn enables the use of a lower-dimensional parameter space characterized as $\mathcal{O}(p\ll 1}$). To build upon these achievements, we propose a novel Bayesian network modeling that not only accounts for the relationship between the underlying physical process and the observable functions, but also captures the connection between the observable functions and the derived variables of interest. By utilizing this model, we are able to utilize sampling techniques to a certain extent, while significantly reducing the computational costs. In addition, our proposed algorithm leverages a combination of sampling techniques and optimization methods to estimate the parameters of the model. We demonstrate the computational efficiency and accuracy of our proposed method, by applying it to the simulation of aeroelastic systems, which involves high-frequency simulation of costly system simulations in an arbitrary-order large system of non-linear ordinary differential equations and maps, and shows improvement over existing approaches. Our proposed method yields a factor of at least $10^2$ improvement in computational cost when compared to the alternative approaches examined in this study, without compromising too much accuracy. Additionally, our proposed method is found to be robust and accurate even when initialized with parameters that have a large deviation from the actual parameters, achieving a significant reduction in error by at least a factor of $10^3$ when compared to the alternative approaches examined in this study. We anticipate our proposed method to have a major impact on the simulation of complex high-dimensional physical processes that involves costly system simulations, due to its high accuracy and the significant reduction in computational cost, making it possible to estimate a large number of parameters in a high-dimensional parameter space. Our proposed method is highly versatile and can be applied to a wide range of applications and is expected to have a major impact on the simulation of complex high-dimensional physical processes that involves costly system simulations, due to its high accuracy

Our research examined the connection between triangular flow $v_3$ and initial anisotropic transverse density in 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions using a multiphase transport model. Our findings show that $v_3$ is directly related to the transverse density in both systems, with a notable difference in the ratio of $v_3/\epsilon_3$ between Au+Au and Cu+Cu at the same $\epsilon_3$. This disparity can be attributed to the influence of nucleon-nucleon collisions on the creation of $K^+$ and $p$ in different centralities. Additionally, we found that $v_3$ is more sensitive to the effects of the vector potential than elliptical flow $v_2$ at midrapidity. Our research also indicates that $v_3$ is more closely aligned with $v_2$ than $p_T$ in Au+Au collisions, with a $v_2/v_3 \propto 1.5$$_{SD}$ dependence on centrality. However, this proportion decreases to approximately 1.2 as $p_T$ increases from 0.4 to 2 GeV/$c$. Our study further reveals that $v_3$ remains independent of $p_T$ within the measured $p_T$ range in Cu+Cu collisions. Our research offers a theoretical explanation using the Wigner distribution function and suggests that $v_3$ may exhibit $p_T$ dependence in higher-energy collisions due to gluon spin polarization. Our findings also suggest that initial anisotropic flow is directly linked to the anisotropic distribution of produced particles in the local rest frame of the medium, which is influenced by the vector potential and serves as a driving force for final-state anisotropic flow. Our research further indicates that the ratio of $v_3/\epsilon_3$ can be used to probe the interaction between quarks and gluons in medium-sensitive collisions. Our study demonstrates that $v_3$ is more sensitive to the effects of the vector potential than $v_2$ in the medium, leading to an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in comparison to $v_2/\epsilon_2$. Our research also shows that $v_3$ and $v_2$ exhibit different $p_T$ dependence in medium-sensitive collisions, with an increasing proportion of $v_2/v_3$ as $p_T$ increases from 0.

Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, which pose both opportunities and challenges for their users. While such datasets provide a solid basis for user-driven applications that utilize semantic search, the quality of these datasets remains unaddressed, which is crucial for ensuring the accuracy of query results and the overall performance of such applications. Regrettably, existing quality assessment methods for Linked Data and RDF datasets are often limited in their scalability due to their focus on detailed, granular evaluations and the lack of advanced computing infrastructure, which are key factors hindering their utilization in a production environment. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel, scalable quality assessment framework specifically designed for evaluating large-scale RDF datasets in an distributed environment. This framework leverages the capabilities of a large cluster of computers to evaluate the quality of an RDF dataset by dividing it into manageable parts, enabling it to handle extremely large datasets with ease and efficiency. Moreover, our proposed method calculates a wide range of quality metrics for each quality aspect, which are subsequently combined into an overall quality score for the dataset, which is ideally suited for a quality-driven (such as quality-aware query processing) use case. We thoroughly evaluate the performance of this framework by conducting a wide-ranging set of experiments utilizing real-world and synthetic datasets, and the experimental results demonstrate its superiority over existing assessment methods in terms of scalability. Furthermore, our proposed method boasts an enhanced level of scalability that enables the assessment of high-quality multi-corpora datasets such as the Lehigh University Benchmark (LUBM) and the YAGO dataset with ease. In particular, our experiments showcase the ability of our framework to handle datasets with up to 10 billion triple descriptions in a distributed environment. Nonetheless, our study reveals that the assessment of large datasets is significantly hindered by the presence of repetitive and redundant data, which poses a significant challenge to any quality assessment method. As a result, our proposed method is ideally suited for evaluating real-world multi-corpora datasets such as the DBpedia, the YAGO, and the German Wikipedia, which comprise up to 10 billion description triplets. Nonetheless, our study highlights the considerable slowdown that quality assessment methods experience when dealing with large datasets containing substantial amounts of repetitive and redundant data. As such, our proposed method is perfectly tailored for the assessment of real-world multi-corpora datasets such as the DBpedia, the YAGO, and the German Wikipedia, which comprise up to 10 billion description triplets

However, this is rarely the case in practice, and researchers are typically limited to analyzing discrete, noisy data. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances is a crucial capability for self-driving cars, given the need to anticipate potential hazards. Unfortunately, their existing detection systems often fall short due to overestimation of range when the objects' dimensions are scale-hypothesized. To address this, a new detection framework called Far3Det is proposed, utilizing a unique approach to estimate object sizes from scratch rather than relying on scale hypotheses. This system also incorporates a special type of anchor box called a far-anchor, designed to match the objects' actual size at a given distance, rather than their perceived size. Before the final decision layer, this system performs a size-aware classification and a distant regression to refine the estimation of object sizes from scratch. Our experimental results using the nuScenes dataset demonstrate that this system outperforms existing detection frameworks when evaluating distant object detection. Furthermore, when tested on a real-world scenario, it successfully identified a distant car and warned the driver, indicating its potential for real-world applications. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/leiming1994/Far3Det for public access. Soft-tissue navigation is increasingly applied in minimally invasive surgery, relying on preoperative imaging that often features non-rigid tissue deformations. Before treatment, registered maps of internal organs are created from multiple imaging sources, which can vary in type and are affected by external factors such as temperature, gravity, and imaging modality, resulting in unpredictable distortions. To overcome these challenges, a new surface-based registration framework has been developed, capable of aligning distorted surfaces without relying on rigid transformations or parametric models. By leveraging B-spline control points that mirror the complexity of actual organ structures, the framework registers surfaces through an energy-based minimization method that prioritizes both geometric similarity and biomechanical properties, thereby producing more accurate and stable results. Compared to established methods, our approach demonstrates superior performance in registering distorted surfaces, as demonstrated by experiments utilizing real and simulated data. Our new algorithm also facilitates real-time execution, essential for its integration into surgical tools that require high processing speeds. Furthermore, our framework has been successfully applied in real-world surgical procedures, showcasing its practical applications and potential. For autonomous navigation and stable motion, estimating scene flow from stereo pairs is crucial. However, due to metric distortions caused by projecting stereo images from 3D to 2D, this task becomes particularly difficult. Existing metric depth estimation methods often overextend their applications to unrelated data, which hinders their performance in the scene flow task. This issue is addressed by our proposed approach, where we develop a unique metric learning technique to circumvent the limitations of projecting stereo images. By incorporating auxiliary tasks that focus on the non-metric aspects of image correspondences, we leverage the strengths of both supervised and self-taught learning. Through rigorous testing on the DTAM scene flow benchmark, our model excels in performance, achieving a median error of 421.34, which outperforms the current best self-taught and robust approach by a significant 10.13, while also demonstrating an 12% improvement in median error when tested on the NYU Depth V2 dataset. A key aspect of our work involves a novel analysis of the challenges and existing approaches in scene flow estimation. In particular, we critique current methods that implicitly rely on correspondence information in training, which hinders their ability to generalize to unrelated scenes. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of robust metric training and outline strategies for achieving it through adversarial and cross-entropy optimization techniques. This paper introduces a new approach called automatic system call rule learning for containerized microservices, enabling the detection of known and unknown malware based on customized rules. Traditional anomaly-based detection methods within Virtualized Extensible Load Module (VELM) environments are ineffective due to their extensive system call monitoring scope and poor performance. In contrast, rule-based detection within these environments offers better performance but requires significant time and expertise from system administrators in determining system call patterns. To address this challenge, a machine learning algorithm called Timeloops is developed to automatically generate system call rule patterns from historical data within a containerized microservice environment. The algorithm leverages a combination of permutation-based feature selection and a decision-tree-based learning approach to optimize the learning process, eliminating the need for feature engineering. Experimental results using the Anubis dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves comparable or better accuracy compared to existing approaches, such as Velmor, Cytosca, and Monodost, while significantly reducing the feature engineering requirement. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has significant applications in geophysical exploration to predict seismic risk and underground resource distribution. Seismic data holds the key to achieving this by mapping subsurface structures, but its analysis is a complex problem due to varying frequency information contained within the data as a result of wave propagation. Traditional migration methods such as Kirchhoff and wave-equation migration that account for wave propagation rely on assumed properties of seismic waves, which may not always accurately hold true, particularly in complex subsurface conditions. A different approach is wave-equation waveform inversion (WEWI), which models seismic data based on the forward problem, but this method is computationally expensive and prone to local minima in the optimization process. WEWI has been successfully applied in simplified scenarios but requires further development to tackle real-world challenges. This study introduces an alternative method called waveform gradient source (WGS) inversion, which splits the data modeling process into two steps: the first generates waveform gradients using the wave equation and the second uses these gradients to update the source wavelets through an inverse scattering problem. This two-step process is equivalent to the full WEWI but is more computationally feasible, enabling the use of larger time and spatial grids, thus producing wavelets that better match real-world seismic data. Furthermore, wavelets obtained through WGS can be stacked over expanded time and frequency windows, providing a more detailed and interpretable result compared to conventional time-migration. We introduce numerical models with heterogeneous and anisotropic media and compare the performance of WGS and conventional time-migration using anisotropic and expanded time windows, demonstrating that the latter yields more accurate and detailed results in both cases. Additionally, we investigate the impact of varying grid sizes on the computation cost, showing that a middle ground yields the best results, and successfully apply WGS to real data from the Marmousi II model and a field data set from the Sigsbee dome. Our results indicate that time-domain expanded source waveform gradient migration yields more detailed and accurate results in comparison to conventional time-migration using anisotropic and expanded time windows, providing a viable method for the interpretation of seismic data set. This method is particularly useful for the imaging of complex structures in exploration and production, such as fault networks and sedimentary basins. Additionally, we successfully apply this method to a 3D data set from the Sigsbee dome, obtaining a detailed and accurate image of this dome. Neural networks can be seen as using multiple linear combinations of its inputs to different outputs. The ability of specific combinations to capture relevant information varies based on the data being used to train the network, whether it's the initial training data or later for tasks like being fine-tuned or being generated on his own from random noise. Some existing approaches that attempt to control which combinations are used have proven to be ineffective when applied to new, unseen data. Our proposed modulated cyclic activation unit addresses this issue by allowing the network to select the most appropriate combinations for each output across different training phases. Not only does it outperform the baseline by improving accuracy, but it also achieves this while reducing the number of parameters. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission individual who interacts with others for an abbreviated period. This research delves into the epidemiological implications of such super-spreader events, where the disease's basic reproduction number is reduced due to the presence of these high-transmission individuals. We analyze the effects of the time the infected person spends among the uninfected, as well as how the probability of an individual becoming infected through contact with an infected person, is influenced. We demonstrate that the occurrence of super-spreader events is crucial in shaping the epidemic's trajectory, and that they can significantly reduce the overall number of infected individuals, while also potentially preventing the epidemic from spiraling out of control if the reproduction number is critical. Furthermore, we find that the model's equilibrium in an open population can result in a stable coexistence between infected and uninfected individuals. The model is further expanded to account for the birth of new individuals, and both deterministic and stochastic variants of the model are considered. Our findings are corroborated by computational simulations using a discrete stochastic model. The introduction of a high-transmitter in an existing population of low-transmitters consistently results in a significant reduction in the overall number of infected individuals, as well as the rapid convergence to an equilibrium where both infected and uninfected individuals coexist steadily. The inclusion of a birth mechanism in the population leads to an increase in the long-term equilibrium population size, and our research provides insight into the intricate interplay between the population's demographic and epidemiological dynamics. The model has implications for understanding the sudden outbreaks that can occur in high-transmission environments, such as music festivals, and highlights the importance of isolating infected individuals who have a high transmission rate. The research suggests that time is a critical factor in managing epidemics, and that even small reductions in the time spent among the uninfected can significantly reduce the reproduction number. The model can be applied across different populations, and the variables can be adjusted to fit the specific characteristics of the population in question. The research provides a framework for understanding the complex dynamics of epidemics, and the influence of individual transmission rates on the spread of the disease. The model can be used to make predictions and recommendations for managing and controlling the spread of the disease, and the inclusion of a birth mechanism in the population models the natural fluctuations that occur in real-world populations. The research highlights the importance of considering the transmission rate of an individual in an epidemic population, and the impact of a high-transmission individual on the spread of the disease.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization abilities of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-based enhancement method known as CATAGE, which exposes models to a diverse range of generated text that represents past experiences.
By incorporating a unique sampling strategy that limits the influence of catagorization, CATAGE successfully prevents the models from exhibiting biased task preferences.
Our experimental results indicate that CATAGE yields significant improvements in generalizing across tasks in an unsupervised setting, with particular strengths in facilitating models' efficient learning and their ability to generalize in a low-data transfer scenario. Moreover, our work showcases the first instance of achieving zero-shot cross-task generalization through model fine-tuning alone. Moreover, our work also includes an attention-aware model the CATAGE-DA variant which achieves the best performance to date in the Natural Language Generation Benchmarks. The proposed method is readily applicable to various transformer-based models and is now publicly available for use as a ready-made framework. With great potential, future research can further explore the implications of our method on model selection, particularly in scenarios involving diverse datasets and various types of tasks. In operating modern artificial intelligence models, particularly those that are cloud-based, there is a constant threat of security breaches resulting in compromised performance and potential malicious instruction issuance. This research focuses on enhancing the long-term security of these models by investigating differential privacy, which safeguards against data-driven attacks. By incorporating private differential privacy protection into deep learning training, the risk of a breach is minimized even if an unauthorized user gains access to the training data. However, introducing noise into the backpropagation computation process hinders the optimization process and complicates the selection of suitable hyperparameters. This research paper proposes an advanced stream processing engine called LifeFlow, which is designed to efficiently handle regular streams by utilizing skillful sorting and efficient skill chaining. Unlike traditional one-pass engines, LifeFlow utilizes a unique hybrid sorting approach that incorporates both external sorting and internal sorting to optimize performance. Based on real-world data, LifeFlow has demonstrated significantly better processing speeds, with up to 3 times faster query execution and reduced memory usage by half, compared to conventional stream processing engines. A real-world application built with LifeFlow has shown a notable memory reduction of 5 times, indicating that this engine is particularly suited for processing regular streams with varying data sizes and time gaps. LifeFlow's capabilities have been further highlighted by its ability to support both aggregation and non-aggregation queries, as well as its potential for further optimization and potential issues with exact sort ordering. A simplified version of LifeFlow, called LifeFlow-L, has also been tested, which uses an in-memory approach for smaller data sets, demonstrating that even this simplified version can still achieve high performance. This research paper was presented at the 2019 IEEE 35th International Conference on Data Engineering, held in Chile. The implementation of LifeFlow as an open-source engine has inspired other research projects, such as LightStream and FlowDB, and its code is now available on GitHub under the Apache License, due to its high efficiency in processing regular streams. Nevertheless, LifeFlow is not designed to handle event streams or continuous queries with unpredictable data arrivals. Furthermore, LifeFlow's performance relies on the precise sorting of data, which can result in slow query execution for certain data sets. Additionally, LifeFlow is not compatible with arriving data that requires immediate processing, such as real-time streams, which necessitates re-sorting of already processed data sets. Lastly, LifeFlow's ability to process regular streams effectively is contingent upon the occurrence of periodic time gaps in its data sets. If such time gaps are absent, LifeFlow's performance may degrade significantly. Nevertheless, LifeFlow remains the first high-efficiency stream processing engine capable of processing regular streams by utilizing a unique hybrid sorting approach that incorporates both external and internal sorting. We introduce a novel approach to regularizing neural networks by imposing a consistent Lipschitz continuity constraint across all layers. Imposing this constraint directly is computationally impractical; instead, we develop an efficient and scalable optimization technique that leverages randomized testing to determine a neural network's Lipschitz constant and incorporates this into a consistent enforcement framework. This framework includes two primary methods for achieving consistent enforcement: one involves introducing a surrogates' enforcement term to the primary network's loss function, while another involves formulating consistent enforcement as a minimax optimization problem. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by achieving state-of-the-art accuracy in image classification tasks, notably surpassing the current best result in the CIFAR-10 dataset, as well as enhancing the robustness of neural networks in various scenarios. Moreover, our approach facilitates model interpretation by providing a measure of the diversity of features extracted by each layer. This diversity metric reveals that our method's enforcement of consistent layer behavior often results in extracted features that are less localized than those produced by traditional neural networks. We publicly release our code and a pre-trained model trained with our approach available at https://github.com/strmline/LCNR. Additionally, we provide an interactive visualization tool for feature maps extracted by our method and conventional neural networks at https://www.strmline.com/lcnr/. This enables visual comparison of our approach's results with those obtained from standard neural networks. Moreover, we introduce a publicly available PyTorch model that incorporates our innovative LCNR method, which achieves a top-of-the-line 94.37% accuracy on the CIFAR-10 dataset. This model serves as a prime example for researchers seeking to explore ways to enhance the robustness of neural networks. By providing clear goals and assessing players' progress, therapeutic applications can leverage the motivational aspects of gaming to enhance the rehabilitation process. Additionally, the feedback loop enabled by performance assessment allows therapeutic applications to adjust difficulty levels and challenge intensity in response to the individual's progress, thereby promoting a sense of self-efficacy and motivating the person to continue with the rehabilitation session. By incorporating the principles of fundamental mechanics, objective functions, and performance feedback into therapeutic gameplay, the potential exists to create more effective and engaging physical rehabilitation therapies, particularly in the treatment of balance-related disorders, muscle relaxation, and motor skill development. This line of reasoning can be seen as an extension of the ideas presented by the proponents of the therapeutic game framework and the concept of serious games, and our proposed model aligns with the principles of challenge investment and flow theory. Moreover, our proposed model and the concepts of therapeutic games and serious games all share common underpinnings with the psychological theory of self-determination, particularly the aspect related to intrinsic motivation. A key aspect of performance feedback in the context of therapeutic gameplay is the choice between subjective self-reporting and more objective biomechanical analysis for assessing an individual's physical rehabilitation progress. The use of self-reporting feedback, often in the form of visual progress indicators within the game, can provide a measure of the motivation derived from playing the game, but may not accurately capture the underlying physical changes. On the other hand, biomechanical analysis offers a more precise measurement of physical rehabilitation progress but may not adequately capture the motivational aspects of playing the game. A balanced approach that combines both subjective self-reporting and objective biomechanical analysis is likely the most effective way to create an optimal and engaging therapeutic game that meets both the physical and motivational requirements of the individual playing it. This combined approach is likely to create a positive feedback loop where the motivation derived from playing the game drives further physical rehabilitation, which in turn is reflected in improved performance, which is then rewarded by the therapeutic game with increased levels of challenge and a higher level of engagement. We develop a variational approximation, utilizing a piecewise-linear map and an absolutely homogeneous functional, which in turn enables the use of Bregman distance for optimization purposes. This allows us to formulate and solve a range of challenging estimation and denoising problems on graphs, lattices, and other structured domains. Our method leverages the properties of absolutely homogeneous functions to introduce a new type of Bregman iteration, which ultimately results in the optimization of a piecewise-stiff map. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through the solution of an image processing task, including a comparison with other approximation techniques. Additionally, we provide a concise algorithm for our proposed method and make use of the structure of our problem to take advantage of specialized solver tools. We also discuss the theoretical convergence of our method and provide a convergence rate of $O(1/N)$. Furthermore, we introduce and solve an innovative problem involving the optimization of a piecewise-linear map subject to a fixed domain constraint. This problem arises as a subproblem in our primary estimation task and involves the optimization of a stiff map on a decreasing sequence of domains. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the solution to this problem and provide a concise algorithm for its solution. This problem also has the added benefit of enabling the use of specialized solver tools, resulting in significant computational efficiency. Our method and its variants provide a valuable solution path for a wide range of application domains, including image processing, optimal design, and mechanics. Our method is also well-suited for the use of high-performance computing tools, allowing for a significant increase in computational efficiency. Our method is implemented using the Theano library and is currently being integrated into the FEniCS project. Our method and its variants provide a robust and flexible solution strategy for a wide range of estimation and optimization problems, and we anticipate that it will be of significant interest to a wide range of application domains and communities. Radiation exposure from CT scans used in medical imaging can be hazardous, especially when used repeatedly on vulnerable populations. Combining low-dose CT scans with PET scans that have similar soft tissue contrast but higher signal-to-noise ratio allows for effective soft-tissue differentiation through multimodal imaging. By training neural networks on such combined data, we can effectively minimize the dose required for CT scans. However, neural networks are prone to overfitting when trained with a limited amount of data, particularly when posed with low-quality scans from unfamiliar scanners. To address these challenges, we developed a novel framework for building models that utilize uncertainly-based residual learning to repair poor-quality training data and incorporate an efficient data augmentation technique to significantly expand the training dataset without the need for additional scans. By applying this framework to a small dataset of low-dose PET scans, we were able to achieve comparable results to previously reported methods, while reducing the dose required by tenfold. Notably, our method demonstrates a high degree of robustness to scanner changes, enabling the creation of models from small datasets of varying backgrounds, thereby greatly expanding the practical applications for reduced-dose PET scans. Furthermore, our method successfully generated images from unseen scanners with a high degree of accuracy, achieving an absolute percentage error of 3.35% when compared to traditionally obtained PET scans, and a PSNR of 35.25, indicating a high quality of reduced-dose PET images. Overall, our framework offers a groundbreaking solution for reduced-dose PET scans, leveraging the synergistic use of CT and PET data to achieve outstanding results. Additionally, it presents an intriguing example of how uncertainty-aware neural networks can be used to tackle real-world medical imaging challenges. Furthermore, our approach is also applicable to other medical low-dose imaging applications involving CT scans, such as reduced-dose CT colonography. The study of operator expansions through the Fa-di-Fa (FF) method and the Wick theorem has been examined in the context of the Minkowski space-time. Investigating the operator $\phi(x)$ at the spacetime point $x$, we aim to express it using an expansion of interacting field operators at distinct spacetime points. We seek to comprehend why this expansion converges to the classical field theory when the spacetime points coincide and the effects of point-like interactions are negligible. Furthermore, we seek to identify the conditions and suitable bases for expansions of operator $\phi(x)$. The Wick theorem proves instrumental in expanding the field operator $\phi(x)$, and the Fa-di-Fa method enables the examination of this expansion's convergence and the proposed basis's efficacy. We also examine potential applications of these theories to the development of renormalizable quantum field theories. The limitations and potential breakthroughs in using these theories to regulate the divergences in quantum field theories are also discussed. Furthermore, the enhanced strategy demonstrated its versatility by generating a universally applicable model, which was found to be robust and adaptable to diverse environments. In the context of limited-label medical image segmentation, a significant challenge lies in effectively utilizing both annotated and unannotated images for training. A key issue here is the efficient allocation of limited annotation across images of varying quality for optimal utilization in a limited dataset. The problem is further compounded by the need to strike a balance between maximizing the utilization of annotated images, leveraging unannotated images via self-supervision, and minimizing the amount of annotation required. In this research, we introduce a novel boundary-conscious information maximization framework that prioritizes regions of high diagnostic value, leverages unannotated images via self-supervision, and reduces annotation demands. The proposed framework is a sequential process, first identifying high-diagnostic-value regions through a unsupervised boundary-aware strategy, followed by the optimization of annotation placement, and finally, the integration of annotated images into the training process. Our experimental results on dermoscopy images demonstrate that our framework achieves superior diagnostic accuracy when compared to existing methods. Additionally, our study reveals that the proposed framework effectively prioritizes region diagnosis based on diagnostic value, thereby leading to enhanced performance. Word sense induction (WSI) aims to divide words with multiple meanings into their respective contexts.
One effective approach to achieving this is through the lexical semantic change detection method, where
the goal is to identify pairs of words that have equivalent meanings based on their context within specific
phrases or documents. Current state-of-the-art techniques primarily employ neural network-based semantic
representation techniques such as BERT and its derivatives; however, these methods are not well-suited for
large-scale word sense induction tasks due to their costly nature. One key challenge lies in developing a
model that can efficiently produce a sense-aware embedding of words across various contexts without
exhausting available memory. Another key challenge lies in the significant overlap existing between different
word senses, which poses a packing problem for the embedding matrix. To address these issues, a novel
approach called Multi-Scale Word Sense Embedding (MS-WSE) has been proposed, utilizing a hybrid of
fine-grained and coarsely-grained representations to capture both the distinct and shared aspects of a word's
meanings. This approach makes use of a combination of neural network-based semantic representations and a
soft-packing strategy to reduce the unnecessary overlap between different word senses. By applying this
strategy to a dataset of lexical semantic change instances, a high accuracy of 89.5% was achieved in the
resulting word sense induction task. Moreover, the proposed MS-WSE framework demonstrated its
efficacy by achieving better or comparable performance when compared to the current leading approaches in the
lexical semantic change detection and word sense induction communities. The model's effectiveness was
further validated across three diverse word similarity tasks, where it consistently outperformed the current
state-of-the-art models. The proposed MS-WSE framework offers a practical solution for the efficient
development of a word sense embedding that can be utilized in a wide range of applications and has the
potential to process large-scale word sense induction tasks efficiently. Furthermore, the framework's
flexibility allows it to integrate multiple neural network-based semantic representation models, which was
demonstrated by incorporating the BERT4WS480 model into the framework, resulting in a further
improvement of 1.2% in the evaluation metric when compared to the baseline approaches. The proposed
MS-WSE framework has the lowest reported parameters among the current leading approaches while
maintaining a high accuracy of 89.5%. The source code of the proposed framework has been made

This reversal is seen as an adjoint process, reflecting an duality between the physical properties of a system and its underlying structural characteristics. This adjoint process is represented as an adjoint functor, capturing the relationship between the geometric and topological properties of a system's configuration space and its associated Hilbert space. This relationship is further elaborated through the use of 2-categorical theory, which allows for an interpretation of the adjoint process as a categorical transformation that is itself an object within a higher-order category. This interpretation provides a meta-level understanding of the adjoint process, one that is invariant and universally applicable. In the context of the Bigoto-Benini-Hull-Witten type gauged supergravity model, the configuration space can be reinterpreted as an Grassmannian geometry, whose geometric properties correspond to a system of Heisenberg algebras. These algebras, in turn, are equivalent to the algebras that define the Hilbert space, providing a direct link between the geometric properties of the configuration space and the structural characteristics of the Hilbert space. The source of gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting gamma-rays remains a mystery.  Had these galaxies been observed at a different time, their gamma-ray emission might not have been detected above a certain threshold, portending a more dynamic gamma-ray activity in these galaxies.  In a study of 56 galaxies classified as low-power radio galaxies, it was found that a subset of 11 galaxies, characterized by having compact radio cores and significant magnetic fields in their surrounding environments, exhibit extreme gamma-ray activity in 20% of observations, while showing little to no gamma-ray activity in the other 80% of observations.  A model explaining gamma-ray activity envisions a situation in which magnetic fields, once linked to the galaxies' central black holes due to accretion, are released when a disk formed from captured material gets too thick, allowing high-energy gamma-rays to emanate as a result of a process in which electrons are accelerated by magnetic fields in the disk.  This model predicts that such a phenomenon should occur at a rate of about once every 10 to 30 years in each of these galaxies, which should have detectable gamma-ray signals only once every 50 to 150 years on average, making them candidates for producing the highest energy gamma-rays observed, above 100 TeV, and potentially increasing the likelihood of gamma-ray absorption in surrounding cool gases if their distance is less than 50 megaparsecs.  Since these galaxies emit gamma-rays in a manner that is temporally variable, and given their consistent production of high-energy gamma-rays, they should also be considered as prominent candidates for sources of extremely high-energy cosmic phenomena such as giant air showers reported by radio listeners, occurring when a gamma-ray beam passes through, which could happen if the galaxy is closer than 12 gigaparsecs, a distance which can vary as the galaxy and the Earth move in their respective cosmic paths.  A prediction based on this model also forecasts that extremely high-energy gamma-rays, above 100 TeV, will be directed towards Earth in about one year's time from a galaxy located 79 megaparsecs away, which is consistent with findings reported by radio listeners of an unusually large giant air shower occurring around that time.  It is further theorized that a similar model explaining gamma-ray activity can be applied to a different, more powerful type of active galactic nuclei, known as flat-spectrum radio quasars, although it may require additional ingredients, such as accretion, to produce gamma-rays and to differ from low-power radio galaxies

Researchers anticipate discovering Pulsar Timing Array signals resulting from merging supermassive black hole binaries with significant orbital eccentricities at a high confidence level. This study delves into the precision of such detections and the computational costs involved. By comparing different computational approaches, our findings suggest that a feasible and accurate method for predicting PTAs signals is through an over-lapping technique of distinct radial patterns in an eccentric system. This method allows for a significant reduction in computational costs, making it an appropriate approach for thorough searches. The precision of searches relying on this method is on par with more comprehensive techniques, at a cost of a modest increase in runtime. This comes with the benefit of a substantial decrease in the computational time, making it an attractive option for searches in larger data sets. Furthermore, our research provides a foundation for further optimization of searches in Pulsar Timing Arrays, specifically in regards to searching for signals from merging black hole binaries with significant orbital eccentricities. This is especially relevant as such signals are anticipated to contribute to nanohertz gravitational wave background, which will be actionable for Pulsar Timing Arrays in the near future. This study is a follow-up to our previous work presented at the 12th Meeting of the Asian Gravitational Society in Seoul, Korea, where an outline of our findings was presented. That earlier presentation resulted in an invitation for our team to participate in a roundtable discussion on Pulsar Timing Arrays at the 9th Numerical Relativity Workshop held in Osaka, Japan, where we had the opportunity to discuss our research with other experts in the field. This current research is an expansion of those earlier findings, and as such an updated version of my previous work has been accepted for presentation at the 3rd Gravitational Wave Astronomy workshop to be held in Hobart, Tasmania in Australia. By integrating a directed network that prioritizes tumor segmentation, the proposed MAG-Net model leverages classification information to guide its tumor segmentation process. The determination of the neutron radius in the ground state of nuclei has been known for over a decade, with values varying significantly depending on the method used. While empirical approaches yield an average square radius of around 46 me$^2$, theoretical models produce a wider range of results. The issue has been extensively explored within the relativistic mean field framework and its non-relativistic counterpart, with recent studies revealing a relatively narrow spread of around 1 me$^2$ when considering various functional forms of the Walecka model and their non-relativistic six-dimensional collective model equivalents. However, a crucial aspect that has not been thoroughly examined in these analyses is the impact of the parameter $k_f$ on the calculation, where $k_f$ represents the Fermi momentum of neutrons within the nucleus. In the present work, we revisit the previous investigations by incorporating a range of $k_f$ values, derived from various effective one-body potentials that maintain consistency with the empirical neutron radius, in order to reassess the spread of the neutron radius. Our results demonstrate that the average square radius of the neutron spread is substantially larger when considering different $k_f$ values, resulting in a spread of approximately 8 me$^2$. Furthermore, we observe a direct correlation between the choice of functional forms and the $k_f$ values, highlighting that the spread of the neutron radius is essentially a reflection of the diversity of theoretical interpretations of the empirical neutron radius, where different $k_f$ values correspond to distinct mean field potentials that can yield unique collective results. Additionally, we find that the average square radius of the neutron spread exhibits a linear relationship with the spread of the single-neutron energy levels, thereby providing a practical indicator for evaluating the dependence of calculations on the choice of functional forms and $k_f$ values. Our study offers a profound understanding of the diversity of theoretical results for the average square radius of the neutron spread in the ground state of nuclei, emphasizing that it is an inherent property that is influenced by the complex interplay between the mean field potential, collective effects, and the unique characteristics of the neutron in-medium density. Consequently, a more precise determination of the neutron radius will necessitate a thorough examination of the underlying theoretical frameworks used in the calculations. Precise and near-real-time forecasting of heavy rainfall and flood-prone areas is severely limited by the time it takes to compute hydrological predictions. Improving computational hydrology requires speeding up numerical methods to minimize trade-offs between model accuracy and processing time. In this study, a novel approach is proposed to achieve a significant increase in efficiency while maintaining a suitable level of detail in the modeling, utilizing the shallow water principle with the highest possible order of spatial and temporal accuracy. A deep learning-based system is developed that utilizes a minimal set of input data, including real-time meteorological information, and utilizes the solver's output as training labels. In practical terms, the proposed deep learning-based model can generate a vast number of predictions in a short period of time, with only a limited number of underlying numerical computations required. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through the application of this technique to the computational hydrology of heavy rainfall events in Umbria and Veneto regions of Italy. The use of this deep learning-based approach led to a 300-fold improvement in processing time, allowing for the generation of 750 predictions per second from a single CPU. The model's performance also shows potential for further optimization and the use of GPU processing. The model has been validated on actual events, with its performance shown in the accompanying videos and figures. The reason for open-sourcing this project is to collaborate with the computational hydrology community and incorporate any novel ideas that may arise from the integration of deep learning and numerical computing. By examining recent proposals and existing implementations utilizing this design, we aim to provide a comprehensive analysis from both theoretical and practical perspectives. Our investigation reveals the underlying reasons for the false sense of security this design provides and highlight the limitations it imposes on parallel processing. Furthermore, we propose a simpler explanation using the false sharing concept, which adequately addresses the performance benefits and drawbacks of the perceived ring buffer design. As a result, any discussion about time and space complexity data structures should incorporate this design's performance, which we advocate should be expressed as a function of the number of blocks rather than an absolute value. Additionally, we outline the implications of our findings for future research in this area. The discussion in this study also raises questions about whether the space complexity of certain data structures, as reported in existing literature, accurately reflects their actual performance. This breakthrough allows us to directly derive a Lyapunov function for these types of systems, providing a mathematical explanation for their asymptotic stability. Our work also explores the use of less restrictive state constraints in the converse theorem, revealing that the specified state constraints do not need to be bounded within a specific shape in order for the asymptotic stability converse theorem to hold. A concrete example is utilized to illustrate the applicability of our findings. Nevertheless, our research offers an early contribution to the study of conversational methods for control systems enabled by continuous state-dependent references. In this paper, we examine the wave equation within the context of quantum mechanics, specifically focusing on the scenario where the potential is mathematically well-defined. Without assuming specific properties of the potential, we derive an isometric mapping that relates the wave equation to a modified stochastic process. This connection enables us to establish a variety of inequalities, including an isometric inequality, which in turn yields inequalities for stochastic integrals expressed in terms of the Hermite operator. Our results also provide a means to establish inequalities for the heat equation when the initial condition has a polynomial form. These inequalities, in turn, allow us to derive bounds for specific expectation values of the wave equation, specifically those involving time and the square of time. These bounds are then applied to derive limits for specific sequences of stochastic processes, leading to a discussion on the type of singular potentials that can be tolerated without the wave equation failing to satisfy an isometric property. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for the modification of the wave equation and the role of time in the Schrödinger equation. In the process, we clarify an earlier argument presented by Kato. Additionally, we identify an error in the literature concerning the application of Bogoliubov's approximation for the ground state of a harmonic oscillator, with the correct interpretation involving the application of a specific transformation before comparison with the results for the stochastic process. Furthermore, we establish an operator-valued analogue of the Hermite function, which in turn enables us to establish a more general inequality for a broader class of operators, including those related to the Dirac operator and the harmonic oscillator. This, in turn, allows us to derive bounds for the expectation values of these operators, leading to a discussion on the type of singular potentials that can be tolerated without the failure of an isometric property of the wave equation. Ultimately, this results in the conclusion that, in order to maintain an isometric property, the potential must be of the type $-m^2$ for the wave equation, $-m$ for the heat equation, and there are no restrictions on the mass parameter $m$ for the stochastic process. This, in turn, raises the question of whether there are any physical interpretations for the mass parameter $m$ in this context. This is addressed in the concluding section in the context of the Schrödinger equation, the harmonic oscillator, and the Dirac operator, with the latter leading to the failure of the isometric property for any non-zero mass parameter. In the context of Assured Information Sharing, the focus is on efficiently sharing verified information between trusted parties while minimizing unnecessary disclosure. This joint effort requires a common understanding of the level of trust among participants, which can be challenging to establish, especially in complex scenarios with high-level concepts and nuanced language descriptions. The issue here is identifying the minimal details necessary for accurate information verification, without over-disclosing sensitive information. To address this difficulty, we propose a novel open-world ambiguity modeling approach, utilizing a hybrid of logical constraints and linguistic analysis to capture the essence of uncertain situations and generate reliable assessments of situation credibility. This approach is particularly useful for handling natural language descriptions of situations, which our evaluation shows can be efficiently applied to scenarios described in multiple languages. Furthermore, our approach is scalable, as demonstrated by our implementation of a prototype using an example domain of navigation, which demonstrates its practical applicability.
