Unlike traditional robotic domains that require extensive and expensive hardware setups for consistent testing, simulation-based environments offer a more cost-effective way to conduct experiments. These advancements permit endless testing of robustness and real-world performance in a controlled setting, allowing for the assessment of demonstration-based methods and  100% coverage of hard-to-reach areas of the state space previously inaccessible with traditional sampling-based approaches. To build upon this progress, we introduce a groundbreaking package called L2Explorer, a cutting-edge suite of continuous 2D navigation tasks that can be used in conjunction with the Gazebo simulation environment and G4T4C, a tool for generating diverse and challenging scenarios through various wind patterns. By integrating a high-performance, distributed simulation engine called Ignition, L2Explorer can handle an unlimited number of trials with minimal system slowdown, even on standard desktop computers. As a result, L2Explorer enables the evaluation of learning-based methods in a robust, diverse range of scenarios and provides a ground for the exploration of novel evaluation protocols that prioritize 100% coverage of the environment by optimizing a variety of existing and custom objectives, such as the number of unique locations visited, the frequency of hard turns, and the distance traveled between specified points, all of which can be tailored to match the characteristics of different application domains. With its versatile features and endless trial capabilities, L2Explorer is an ideal platform for the assessment of learning-based methods in complex domains and promotes the use of challenge-specific protocols that prioritize diversity and coverage. By leveraging this evaluation ecosystem, researchers can ensure a more rigorous and fair comparison of different approaches and algorithms, while also providing a valuable service to the broader robotics community by openly sharing the results obtained with this platform. Furthermore, we introduce an accompanying dataset that showcases the performance of multiple state-of-the-art reinforcement learning baselines on a diverse set of challenging scenarios, enabling the direct evaluation and comparison of novel methods against this established benchmark. localization occurs in contrast to the non-quasiperiodic case. Studies have
shown that discrete one-dimensional quasiperiodic arrangements usually
accommodate a localized mode around a specific frequency. Notably, lattice
disorder can transform this mode into a rogon-like state, indicating a
delocalized mode existence. Our theoretical and experimental analyses reveal
that mode localization can shift back to a specific frequency range when the
quasiperiodic disorder is sufficiently intense, a phenomenon we term the
delocalization shift. We observed this shift in the spectral characteristics
of the passive microwave system and photonic quasiperiodic arrays it represents
and found the delocalization shift to occur at a disorder intensity equal
to the quasiperiodic strength in one-dimensional settings. The delocalization
shift has implications for the design of passband filters that prevent wave
localization. Furthermore, our results suggest that the hybrid state formed
from the combination of a rogon and a flat band has a higher localization
length than either the rogon or flat band individually. Moreover, the
delocalization shift can be facilitated by introducing a small amount of
symmetry breaking in the quasiperiodic arrangement, a feature that can be
exploited in the creation of wave packets with a high localization length. 
The proposed concept of the delocalization shift may also find applications
in the development of localized minigaps within one-dimensional quasiperiodic
metamaterials. Our study offers a comprehensive analysis of the interplay between
localization and the non-crystalline structure in one-dimensional quasiperiodic
arrays, a phenomenon that could have a significant impact on the design of
discrete photonic structures. Additionally, our results may provide a route
to constructing localized states within one-dimensional quasiperiodic systems. 
Our findings are further verified using a passive microwave structure, a setup
that is also used for the experimental observation of the delocalization shift.

An individual who makes a mistake out of ignorance may still suffer from the consequences of that error, even if they take corrective action. In the case of incorrect statements made on social media, simply removing the false information may not suffice, as the damage is already done. This concept can be applied to a framework of dynamic fuzzy automata, where an agent that has made an incorrect observation due to a fault can rectify the issue with a new, more accurate reading, despite the fact that the incorrect observation still holds. We demonstrate the ability of this agent to recover over time, even if its recovery is marred by further errors, as long as these subsequent mistakes are less significant than the initial one. This achievement generalizes previous success cases, considering the new condition that the agent's ability to correct itself is not unlimited, as there are constraints on the maximum scope of its self-correction, which we express mathematically as $\delta \prececs \lambda$. This advancement in the field of fault-tolerant learning agents is showcased through an example of search repair, where we show that the method outperforms a comparable non-self-correcting agent. Furthermore, we explore additional capabilities of this agent, such as its ability to learn from a teacher that provides correct outcomes, as well as its capacity for complex decision-making in scenarios like the 'paradox of choice'. This includes the scenario where selecting the best option among several equally desirable outcomes may still allow one of these outcomes to cause harm, as a result of the agent's learning from its environment. This learning agent can also navigate more intricate settings, such as multi-fault settings, as well as settings where the agent's learning is influenced by both its own actions and external factors. This results in a more intricate system of interaction, which we refer to as a 'web of faults'. This, in turn, allows for a broader exploration of the concept of repair in the context of learning agents, as it highlights the potential for these agents to address not only single faults but also more complex issues arising from interconnected faults. This includes both static and dynamic types of multi-fault settings, as well as settings where the presence of learning agents contributes to an endless cycle of the agent's observations, actions, and subsequent observations, which we refer to as an 'omnitemporal web of faults'. This cycle raises even more intricate questions regarding how these agents should be expected to behave over time, as it adds another dimension to the already complex issue of how they should be expected to behave over time

We employ this strategy to develop a novel dual-task learning pipeline, where simultaneously training a model to avoid incorrect associations and accurately identify target objects within a given category allows it to overcome the issue of false positives. Our results demonstrate substantial improvements in performance across multiple metrics and a marked reduction in error rates when testing models in real-world scenarios. Notably, our proposed approach achieves particular success when applied to complex situations involving multiple objects. Our implementation and data also serve as a significant contribution, as they showcase unique features such as diverse distributions of target objects and instances of conflicting associations that were previously unexplored areas. This study introduces a novel action recognition dataset called HCMC-CF, which is created from a collection of home security videos.  Due to the limited number of high-quality training videos for each class and the common occurrence of low-light conditions in these scenarios, a unique recognition approach called Delta Sampling R-BERT has been developed.  This approach involves two innovative techniques: first, a method to automatically select more distinctive frames for each video clip by computing frame uniqueness; second, a way to incorporate dark frame segments into the training process using a simple but effective strategy called the Average Masking Method.  Experimental results show that Delta Sampling R-BERT achieves superior performance on the HCMC-CF dataset and outperforms competing methods on several benchmark datasets.  Notably, this approach surpasses state-of-the-art benchmarks like R-GCN and TSM on the ActivityNet by a significant margin, also demonstrating an impressive $11.15\%$ improvement on the human evaluation standard and the ability to effectively utilize dark video segments for training.  Furthermore, this approach shows great potential for adapting to other constrained action recognition datasets due to its ability to effectively utilize limited, dark, and noisy training data.  By applying this method, a model trained on the HCMC-CF dataset achieves a notable $8.21\%$ human evaluation standard and $6.15\%$ frame accuracy on the CMU-16 dataset, a $5.14\%$ human evaluation standard and $3.59\%$ frame accuracy on the PKU-MMD dataset, and a $3.21\%$ human evaluation standard and $2.38\%$ frame accuracy on the UCf-11 dataset.  Due to its effectiveness, this approach is considered a strong candidate for solving low-light action recognition tasks.  The HCMC-CF dataset and Delta Sampling R-BERT implementation are made available to the research community.  By utilizing a pre-trained R-BERT model as a feature extractor and leveraging light and noisy training data, this approach achieves comparable performance to model fine-tuned with action recognition architectures on several benchmark datasets.  However, due to some details being unclear or not explicitly stated, further clarification may be required from the authors. We have derived new propagation characteristics for the linearized equations governing viscous relativistic fluid dynamics. These propagation characteristics are particularly useful for identifying and analyzing wave modes within relativistic fluid systems, and can be applied to both neutral and charged fluids across a wide range of frequencies. We have determined the conditions under which viscous forces are significant and have found that the relativistic correction to the adiabatic index occurs only at very high frequencies. Additionally, we have derived a simplified approximation of the propagation characteristics that can be used for a wide range of applications. This includes developing a linearized version of the Raychaudhuri equation, which relates fluid dynamics to gravitational wave physics, allowing for a more straightforward analysis of gravitational signal modification due to viscous effects. We have further investigated the viscous impact on gravitational wave waves and found that our propagation characteristics accurately capture the behavior of waves across a wide range of frequencies and temperatures. These findings have important implications for the analysis of relativistic fluid dynamics within heavy ion collision and cosmological contexts. Moreover, we have observed that the propagation characteristics can also be applied to relativistic magnetohydrodynamics, making our study relevant to a broader range of electromagnetic fluid systems. Additionally, we have found that the condition for local equilibrium can be expressed in a more intuitive form using the propagation characteristics, further highlighting their utility. Our study provides a comprehensive framework for analyzing wave modes and viscous effects within a wide range of relativistic fluid systems. Deep learning-based anomaly detection on raw data from complex systems has shown great promise in identifying irregularities not yet defined by experts.  By leveraging deep learning's ability to capture data patterns, these methods can effectively pinpoint patterns that don't fit the norm.  However, when working with quantum data, the usual approaches must be reevaluated due to the unique characteristics of this data, such as continuous inputs and probabilistic outputs from a unit sphere.  Existing work on quantum anomaly detection has primarily focused on supervised methods but has overlooked the potential of unsupervised, progressive learning-based approaches.  By combining a quantum data preprocessing module with a deep learning builder that accommodates a non-Euclidean metric, we successfully developed an unsupervised quantum anomaly detection framework called InQMAD.  By progressively learning to distinguish normal and irregular patterns in quantum data, InQMAD leverages an initial, coarse clustering and refines its understanding through a series of nested balls with decreasing radii, representing the learned irregularities.  We applied InQMAD to two challenging scenarios: identifying irregular states in quantum circuits and detecting anomalies in quantum images, and the method outperformed the existing state-of-the-art quantum anomaly detection literature in both cases.  Furthermore, InQMAD's progressive learning nature enables it to successfully detect rare irregularities in large datasets.  We also explored the practical applications of InQMAD on quantum device debugging and quantum chemistry analysis, and the framework's code is openly available for use.  By achieving significant improvements in anomaly detection accuracy on various quantum datasets, InQMAD is a crucial breakthrough for the field of quantum technology.  As quantum technology continues to evolve at a rapid pace, InQMAD's innovative design will likely have a profound impact on the development of future quantum systems.  In the context of machine learning, InQMAD's success story highlights the value of exploring diverse metric spaces and adapting deep learning builders to suit specific data types.  As a result, InQMAD will likely inspire a new wave of research aimed at developing more effective anomaly detection methods for other complex data systems.  Although InQMAD has already shown great promise in identifying irregular quantum states and wave functions, the method's robustness needs to be evaluated across different quantum scenarios.  Furthermore, InQMAD's performance often comes with a higher computational cost, which could impede its real-time applications in quantum technology.  To realize the full potential of InQMAD, future research should focus on enhancing the method's efficiency while maintaining its exceptional anomaly detection accuracy.

This decision sparked a heated debate among legal experts and cryptographers about whether individuals can be forced to decrypt their own encrypted data. Some argued that this would be equivalent to providing a plaintext version of the encrypted information, while others contended that it's essentially the same as being asked to perform a computation on the encrypted data. This paper proposes a straightforward method to validate the authority's demand for decryption independently of their computational perspective. If our proposed protocol aligns with the required computation demanded by the authority, then the outcome is already established. If not, we can determine the authority's intention is either impractically insecure or unnecessarily intrusive. This approach implicitly highlights the inherent value in cryptographers' perspective on this issue. This concept can potentially be applied to a broader range of scenarios involving computation-driven demands from authorities. Furthermore, this paper introduces two general categories for authority demands: those that can be verified by the individual being asked (e.g., decrypting their own encrypted data) and those that cannot be verified by the individual (e.g., providing a signature on a specific message). We demonstrate that classically, any implementation of MDI-QKE can be equivalently represented by a classical two-party key exchange (CPE) based on the principle of privacy amplification, without loss of generality. Furthermore, we show that any CPE generating secure keys can be converted into an secure MDI-QKE protocol. This conversion process involves the utilization of entangled states in a manner that ensures the privacy of the exchanged classical information. As a result, we conclude that the classically equivalent representation of MDI-QKE is universally applicable and of inherent security, thereby providing a fundamental understanding of the underlying properties of this protocol. Moreover, our work enables the development of novel MDI-QKE protocols by leveraging the conversion procedure, allowing for the creation of secure and efficient key exchange protocols based on the utilization of entangled states, without which the corresponding CPE would be vulnerable to certain attacks. The rapid dissemination of information on social media has created an environment in which false news can spread quickly. To address this issue, a significant amount of research has focused on false news detection, particularly using deep learning techniques. While these studies have achieved high accuracy in detecting well-known false news, there is a more challenging problem to tackle: detecting completely new false news that has not been identified before. To address this issue, we propose a new framework called the Multimodal Emergent Counterfeit News Detection Meta Neural Process Network, which learns from established false news data and can generate new descriptions and classification information for unseen false news based on limited metadata. This framework combines a Meta-Gradient Neural Process Network with a Multimodal Neural Process Network, using a meta-learning approach to find the optimal model parameters and producing a point estimate for the classification of new false news. To evaluate our proposed framework, we created a new false news dataset containing 1200 established and 600 new false news articles. Our experiments show that our framework effectively detects completely new false news, achieving an accuracy of 82.34%, which significantly outperforms a strong baseline. Furthermore, our framework's ability to generate new descriptions for false news has been evaluated using human-assisted word similarity evaluation, which indicates that our proposed framework can generate plausible and accurate descriptions for new false news. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/ghrua/MCNPN. For long-form video and audio content, our framework can also use temporal and spectral features in addition to text, which further enhances its performance. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on not only point-estimate accuracy but also on few-shot learning for false news datasets. Our method's strong performance in low-shot learning settings makes it particularly suitable for emerging false news classification. Our method's code and dataset are also available at https://github.com/ghrua/MCNPN. Moreover, our experiments demonstrate that our proposed framework successfully integrates both neural process and meta-learning techniques, producing a model that not only excels in false news detection but also serves as a good example of the benefits of neural process methods in deep learning. Complex systems consisting of interconnected components, often found in social and biological networks, exhibit intricate behaviors resulting from their unique structure and individual characteristics. Due to the intricate interactions between these components, a typical element may be influenced by a diverse range of entities, making it challenging to model their collective dynamics using conventional methods based on linear nearest neighbors. To effectively capture the nonlocal connections and unique characteristics of each component, Graph Neural Networks can provide a more comprehensive understanding of complex systems, enabling the exploration of their structural properties and the discovery of underlying mechanisms and key factors. In this work, an in-depth analysis is conducted of how Graph Neural Networks can model the structural aspects, the distinct features of each component, and the overall system dynamics, leading to a discussion on future research opportunities and applications for both theoretical analysis and real-world problems. Our discussion spans across three main aspects: (1) the identification of suitable multi-layer Graph Neural Networks, such as Graph Attention Networks and Deep Graph Neural Networks, capable of extracting a complex system's structure and component characteristics; (2) the exploration of how these networks can capture a system's dynamics, including the determination of network topology, the identification of latent variables, and the estimation of system parameters; and (3) the presentation of several case studies and real-world applications for complex systems, including our own investigation of corporate stock price dynamics and the underlying mechanisms of cancer gene networks. Our research demonstrates that Graph Neural Networks offer a versatile and effective framework for modeling complex systems, predicting the behavior of cancer gene networks, and identifying key factors influencing corporate stock prices. Additionally, our work highlights the fundamental differences between learning a complex system's architecture and its dynamics, emphasizing the need for a comprehensive approach that considers both structure and component characteristics. Furthermore, our research showcases the broad applicability of Graph Neural Networks to a wide range of fields, including physics, biology, finance, and social sciences, and highlights the numerous open research questions and challenges awaiting the Graph Neural Networks community. Our work also demonstrates the value of a collaborative approach between domain experts and Graph Neural Networks researchers, as well as the importance of open-source implementations and reproducibility in complex systems research. In conclusion, our discussion highlights the significant contributions that Graph Neural Networks can make in better understanding complex systems and their underlying dynamics and structure, and we anticipate that our analysis will inspire future advancements in this field. Our research is also a testament to the power of machine learning and mathematics in driving a new generation of interdisciplinary science and research. To improve upon traditional image segmentation methods, a new type of model has been proposed that directly creates realistic brain lesion images from healthy brain images. By generating authentic lesions, these models can automatically produce lesion masks that mirror actual lesion characteristics, enabling more effective and robust training. To overcome the limitations of simply producing arbitrary images, a type of Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) was adapted to produce lesioned brain images that adhere to the same statistical distribution as actual lesioned images. To reduce raw image dimensions during generation, a type of progressive encoder was incorporated, allowing the model to generate high-quality images from compressed latent codes. To prevent uncontrolled code variations, a gradient penalty was added to the generator's loss function, while also incorporating a adversarial component to evaluate the realism of generated images. By utilizing both a generator and encoder, this type of Variational Adversarial Auto-Encoder (VAAE) was able to produce high-quality lesioned images by first compressing brain images into a meaningful latent code and then expanding this code back into a realistic lesioned brain image. By training this model on a large dataset of brain images with varied lesion types and characteristics, it was found that it could effectively capture the complexity of real lesioned brain images. Notably, this model was found to generate higher-quality lesion masks than traditional segmentation methods, while also producing lesion images that closely mimic actual lesioned brain images. To validate the model's performance, a simple lesion detection algorithm was applied to both real and generated image datasets, showing that it achieved comparable results on both, indicating that the model's generated lesion masks are as effective as real masks. Furthermore, by incorporating a style transfer component, the model was able to generate high-quality lesion images that not only statistically resemble actual lesioned brain images but also accurately replicate the unique appearance and characteristics of specific brain lesions. To demonstrate the model's versatility, it was successfully applied to generate lesioned brain images for various types of lesions, such as cerebral small vessel disease, lacunes, and strokes, without the need for any major modifications. To facilitate widespread use and integration of this model into clinical practices and research, a user-friendly GUI-based toolkit was developed, allowing healthcare professionals and researchers to easily generate high-quality lesioned brain images from healthy brain scans for educational purposes, clinical trials, and educational tools. By providing an accessible and user-friendly interface for modifying the model's parameters and adjusting the generated lesion images to match specific clinical requirements, the toolkit makes this technology easily adoptable for any MRI sequences and brain lesion types.

This article explores recent developments in nonlocal diffusion models, emphasizing how these models can be formulated using integro-differential operators that adhere to physically motivated boundary conditions. Such boundary conditions, which mirror the properties of fractal sets, guarantee that models exhibit desirable symmetry properties and can be accurately approximated by local equations in their smoothest regions. We also discuss how these models can be linked to classical parabolic and elliptic equations in their respective limits, and we provide an overview of available bibliotropy, together with some open questions in the field. Further, this article investigates the potential for casting fractional Sobolev spaces as limits of standard Sobolev spaces, and it proposes alternative approaches for tackling fractional problems involving nonlinear determinants. Ultimately, our aim is to offer a comprehensive examination of the most up-to-date research in this field, encompassing both the abstract theoretical developments and the concrete applications. Some promising new results are obtained, albeit in a rather incidental manner.

Here, the discussion is focused exclusively on the fractional diffusion models themselves. 
  We start by presenting a generic formulation for local and nonlocal diffusion models that incorporate boundary operators, followed by an exploration of the key requirements for these models to display coherent local and fractional limits. This discussion is then utilized to review a diverse range of specific models, beginning with the fractional Laplace operator and its integral kernel, as well as the Mieusse-Tolmeti fractional Hardy-Sobolev inequality. Next, we examine how to approach problems involving nonlinear operators, such as the fractional Allen-Cahn and Fucik equations. In addition, we discuss how to tackle fractional problems involving fractional mean curvature, Ambrosio-Taylor diagrams, and the fractional Sobolev embedding inequality. A common thread throughout these discussions is the crucial role that measure and capacity play in defining and analyzing the fractional limits of these models. Our article concludes with an exploration of the relationship between fractional spaces and the classical Lebesgue space L^1. Here, we establish that fractional Sobolev spaces can be seen as the dual of L^1, which in turn allows for a broader interpretation of the fractional Laplace operator as a duality-based extension of the classical Laplace operator. Our research utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies (U/LIRGs) within a distance of 180 Mpc, all at a redshift of less than 0.04, which are part of the GOALS survey. Our data consisted of an optical spectrum with a wavelength range of approximately 3700 to 4500 A, allowing us to measure the oxygen-based star formation rate and stellar mass. From our findings, we distinguished three types of star formation patterns based on the distribution of star formation: (1) galaxies with star formation confined to the central region, (2) galaxies with star formation in both the central and peripheral areas, and (3) galaxies with no measurable star formation. When comparing these categories, we discovered that the relationship between star formation rate and stellar mass varies significantly among them. Moreover, we detected 11 KDCs (kiloparsec-scale starbursting nuclei) with large star formation rates and found that 5 of these were interacting with a central dust ring, offering a possible explanation for the formation of dust structures in the center of some galaxies. Our research highlights the effectiveness of optical IFU observations in analyzing the physics of galaxy interactions and mergers. Further observations are necessary to fully explore the diversity of star formation patterns in galaxy interactions and mergers and the formation of KCNs. Our data also emphasizes the importance of combining optical IFU observations with radio continuum observations to gain a comprehensive understanding of galaxy physics. Satellite-based imagery is a reliable method for making such predictions, with multi-class classifiers offering a practical solution. However, utilizing traditional machine learning models for this purpose is limiting due to the high cost of obtaining labeled data, a typical challenge in image classification tasks. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that weather conditions can be accurately predicted with a 75% success rate when using a simplified classification strategy. Separating individual speech signals from mixed audio recordings, especially in scenarios with only one audio source available (single-mixed condition), has proven to be a challenging task for speech separation technologies. Current methods typically apply convolutional or recurrent models to extract spectral features and then perform separation, yet they often struggle to effectively utilize information across specific frequency bands. This study introduces dual-path models that combine two unique convolutional recurrent architectures - one focused on general spectral feature extraction and another tailored to processing individual frequency bands - to enhance speech separation performance. Experimentation revealed that a dual-path model employing parallel convolutional and recurrent components yielded superior results, outperforming existing methods in the single-mixed condition according to the BSS Eval toolkit's criteria. Furthermore, this model demonstrated superiority over its single-path counterparts in both clean and noisy environments. The proposed dual-path model has been referred to as DPCRN. To facilitate training and prevent overfitting, a dual-path strategy involving data augmentation was also explored and showed positive results in separating speech from mixed audio recordings. DPCRN has been found to excel in separating speech from mixed audio recordings in both clean and noisy environments. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS upgrade for the upcoming High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC), a new generation of silicon pixel sensors is being developed to enhance the detector's capability to process complex data in anticipation of higher collision rates. Although fully-depleted CCDs were initially considered for use in the forward section of the CMS detector, featuring very low noise and excellent signal-to-noise ratio, they were ultimately rejected due to manufacturing limitations. As a result, the CMS collaboration opted for the development of specialized pixel chips, such as the CMS Phase-1 Pixel Prototype, which were designed to operate in the forward section of the CMS detector. This paper presents the design, production details, and test results of the CMS Phase-1 Pixel Prototype modules, specifically focusing on a particular prototype featuring a 8-slice 3D CMOS readout design and describing the associated reconstruction challenges. Additionally, this paper includes the results of test beam experiments conducted using a prototype module with an active area of 1 cm^2 and comprising 8 individual 250 um thick silicon sensor slices, mounted on a hybrid readout chip. The experiment revealed that the 3D readout chip effectively reconstructed particle hits even when operating with a relatively high hit occupancy induced by high-energy particles. However, the results also showed that the reconstruction performance of the detector declined in areas with the highest hit densities, primarily due to the occurrence of particle hits located within the same 50 nanosecond time frame, as dictated by the hit finding algorithm. As a result, the particle hits in these areas could not be properly separated by the detector, resulting in an increase in the nearby hit densities. To mitigate this issue, the hit finding algorithm was modified to account for time-overlap, thereby enabling the proper separation of particle hits even in areas with the highest hit densities. Consequently, the reconstructed particle tracks demonstrated an enhanced precision, with an average R-phi of 0.6. Furthermore, the results showed that the hit reconstruction efficiency remained above 95% even in areas with hit densities as high as 14 hits per square millimeter. Moreover, the results of the test beam experiments revealed that the hit reconstruction time was consistent across different hit densities, as well as in areas with different amounts of nearby hit densities. The proposed method is illustrated by analyzing the SU(2) glueball spectrum for a specific set of interpolating fields. The results indicate the existence of a scalar state within the mass range $1.50 < m_{\text{S}} < 1.56$ GeV, consistent with the prediction made using an lattice lattice gauge theory model. Furthermore, the study reveals the spectral density's characteristics in the low-mass region, which is found to adhere to the $1/m^3$ law predicted by chiral perturbation theory for two degrees of freedom. The findings of this study are relevant to the ongoing research aimed at detecting the $\eta$ glueball candidate reported by the lattice QCD collaboration, which relies heavily on this spectral density. The results of this study are confirmed by an alternative method that involves analyzing correlation functions via a Lagrange multiplier, which enforces the interpolating field's null ward identity. This method provides a spectral sum rule that is equivalent to the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density. The validity of this method is verified through a comparison with the proposed lattice QCD approach. The proposed method offers a practical solution for extracting the spectral density from correlation functions, which is currently being applied to various research projects. Evaluating public opinion through sentiment analysis on social media platforms like Twitter is increasingly significant for businesses, organizations, and governments in making informed decisions. As a result, there is rising interest in developing effective sentiment analysis systems using machine learning techniques. Sentiment analysis on Twitter poses unique challenges due to the brevity of the text, use of abbreviations, and presence of multiple hashtags in each post. Furthermore, a reliable model needs to accurately identify and analyze both positive and negative language within the same sentence. Characterized by their simplicity and capability to handle time-series data, LSTM networks have become highly versatile in the field of natural language processing. This paper proposes an LSTM-based system for sentiment analysis on Twitter, where each character in the text is represented as a unique embedding that captures grammatical and semantic context. Moreover, the proposed system is able to analyze short text sequences, such as tweets, containing both affirmative and dismissive language within the same sentence. The proposed system's efficacy is validated through a sentiment classification experiment on a Twitter dataset, and the results indicate that the LSTM model outperforms existing approaches like softmax and tree-based methods like random forest and gradient boosting. The source code for the proposed system has been made available on GitHub, providing users with a starting point for adapting the model to suit their specific requirements. The Microscope space mission, launched in 2010, aimed to test the weak equivalence principle by comparing the Earth's gravitational influence on two test masses as the planet rotates. The mission's primary goal was to determine a specific limit on the relative acceleration between the masses, which could indicate a violation of the weak equivalence principle. The mission's data showed an acceptable limit, but was compromised by technical issues known as glitches that occurred during its operation. The analysis of the data lasted seven years and resulted in 15 identified glitches lasting between 2 seconds and 976 seconds. The analysis assumed that the system's behavior during glitches was random and independent of the mission's parameters. By comparing the statistical significance of the test without the data from the glitches, it was found that they had a negligible impact on the results. The analysis of the data, including the glitches, using a different statistical approach also yielded the same limit on the relative acceleration between the masses. The occurrence of the glitches during six specific periods of the mission reduced their impact, but the reason for their causes remains unknown. The analysis of the mission's data demonstrates that the technique used is effective in detecting the violation of the weak equivalence principle, but more powerful experiments are necessary to make significant progress in this area of research. The mission's data was available until a sudden and persistent glitch occurred during its final days of operation. The recent Gravity Probe Gauss experiment has since built upon the achievements of the Microscope mission. The formal evaluation of the mission's data results in the constraint $|{\Delta}/{\bar{\rho}}|< 2.4\times 10^{-12}$, where $\Delta$ represents the allowed variation in the ratio of the densities of the two test masses and $\bar{\rho}$ is the average density of the test masses. The most influential glitch, GA01, reduced the constraint by half but still fell short of the theoretical limit imposed by quantum gravity at the Planck scale. The formal analysis of the data in the framework of the Michaelis model, which is commonly used in quantum gravity, also resulted in the same constraint on the data. The analysis of the data in the context of the Big Bang Theory, specifically during the era of matter domination, tightened the constraint even further but still fell short of the quantum gravity limit at the Planck scale. The analysis of the data in the context of the Brans-Dicke theory of gravity also tightened the constraint, but the model's parameters were found to be inconsistent with the established empirical constraints. Soft condensed matter systems that combine rapidly moving colloidal particles and inhomogeneous activity fields exhibit complex, non-equilibrium behavior. The interaction between these factors produces varied effects such as accelerated sedimentation, altered suspension dynamics, and changed aggregate formation. The influence of activity gradients on colloidal particles is a significant topic that has been investigated through the principles of active suspensions and non-equilibrium thermodynamics. This focus paper delves into the dynamic response of colloidal particles to varying activity gradients, reviewing the applicable theories and presenting a simplified model that captures the complex phenomena observed in active suspensions. The discussed theories explain observed behavior, including how activity gradients impact particle motion, and the mechanisms that drive the aggregation of suspended particles. Furthermore, these theories provide a framework for understanding the intricate interplay between the activity gradient, particle density, and surface roughness in determining the dynamic behavior of colloidal particles in an environment affected by an external force. The discussed phenomena are particularly relevant to the study of biological systems that incorporate moving particles within complex environments and suggest avenues for further exploration in the physics of active suspensions. The scope of this focus paper is primarily restricted to static and dynamic aspects in an attempt to provide an in-depth analysis of the subject matter. The discussion is complemented by an appendix that addresses additional aspects related to the dynamics of colloidal particles under influence of an external force, surface roughness, and how the presented model can be used to derive the stress tensor of an active suspension. The minimum strong shortest route union cover problem has significant implications in optimal mobile flat pricing and dynamic source location problems. To tackle this challenge, we examine a generalized problem that can be applied to any connected graph and consider two specific cases: when the graph is a series of series-parallel trees and when it represents a geographic region. By using the concept of a k-strong shortest path set, where the distance between any two nodes is the shortest distance among k possible routes, we determine the optimal coverage using the fewest number of such paths. Our analysis for the first case shows that covering all nodes with 2-strong shortest paths requires no more than 11 covers, and we provide a cover using 5 such paths in a random scenario. For the second case, we prove that covering all nodes with k-strong shortest paths is an NP-complete problem and present a general method for covering all nodes with an optimal number of 2-strong shortest paths through a heuristic algorithm based on the highest degree first rule. Our results for the first case show that covering all nodes with 2-strong shortest paths requires no more than 12 covers in a random scenario and with an expected value of 5.4 when following the highest degree first rule. Our research on a random scenario with 20 nodes shows that covering all nodes with 2-strong shortest paths requires no more than 8 covers and our results for the second case through a heuristic algorithm based on the highest degree first rule cover all nodes with 4 such paths in a random scenario. Our analysis for a specific instance of a graph that represents a geographic region with 25 nodes through a heuristic algorithm based on the highest degree first rule shows that covering all nodes with k-strong shortest paths requires no more than k*(log(k))^(1/lambda) covers and our results cover all nodes with 4-strong shortest paths with a cover of approximately 4.08 in a random scenario. Nonetheless, in numerous real-world scenarios, annotating data with accurate labels is a time-consuming and costly process. As a result, the aim of the experiment involves investigating the hypothesis that models trained on a limited dataset with high noise levels can achieve comparable performance to models trained on a large, well-annotated dataset, without the need for additional training. The experiment utilizes a black-box framework based on decision-based queries, where queries with diverse semantics are utilized to obtain labels for the data in an unsupervised manner, without requiring additional annotation. The experiment leverages the SuperGlue framework that facilitates semantic matching between data, enabling the application of label spreading and graph-based methods to obtain final predictions. The results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, with improvements ranging from 1.3% to 6.5% in accuracy, depending on the model and dataset used. Achieving optimal policy performance using imitation learning (IL) with limited or poor quality demonstrations is a significant challenge. The demonstrations may contain significant errors, inconsistencies, and irrelevant information, which efficiently transfer to the next task through interpolation is not guaranteed. This research addresses the issue of transferring learned policies to new settings by assuming the demonstrations are of poor quality and contain a significant amount of unnecessary information. The framework is evaluated using the Fetch imitation task, a simple navigation task, and a series of difficult kitchen tasks. The results show that TRAIL successfully learns a close-to-ideal policy using inadequate data. The code for the paper can be found at https://github.com/robot-iis/trail. The first metric measures the minimum number of errors an encoded message can undergo in transit, while the second metric indicates the minimum number of modifications required to convert an ordinary low-density parity-check (LDPC) code into a PAC code. We then investigate various methods for designing and analyzing PAC codes using these metrics, focusing particularly on an effortless approach to enhance the performance of a given LDPC code by converting its check nodes into PAC check nodes. By utilizing graphical representation and density evolution, we demonstrate the efficacy of this conversion strategy, followed by a theoretical justification of its effectiveness from a computational perspective. Notably, this conversion allows for the alteration of check node functions without needing a corresponding change in the decoding algorithm, thus enabling the creation of PAC codes with superior performance characteristics from existing LDPC codes. We also present a straightforward procedure for implementing this conversion method. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the relationship between the two performance metrics of PAC codes and identifies the optimal conditions under which the conversion strategy achieves the best results. Finally, we showcase the applicability of this conversion method to large-scale systems by enhancing the performance of a 5G New Radio (NR) communication standard code, resulting in a further reduction of error rates. By combining this conversion strategy with a more advanced version of density evolution, it becomes feasible to compute the optimal enhancement levels for individual check nodes, thereby further improving the performance of the designed PAC codes. In the context of 3D medical image analysis, partial volumetric effects frequently distort diagnostic features, compromising the accuracy of deep learning-based segmentation models. This difficulty is compounded by the substantial annotated data required for training deep learning models, a common challenge in radiology applications. To address these obstacles, we propose an innovative Edge-Gated CNN (EG-CNN) framework that leverages implicit edge information for lightweight training and subsequent segmentation of contaminated volumetric data. The EG-CNN framework integrates two primary components: an Edge-Gated 3D (E-G3D) module and a Successive Transverse Slice (STS) module. The E-G3D module, inspired by the success of edge-aware image fusion methods in capturing implicit information, is employed to learn edge information from partial slices. This learned information is then used to guide the STS module, comprising a series of 2D CNNs that leverage this knowledge to segment contaminated volumetric data by combining transverse slices. Through the inclusion of an implicit edge-aware branch, the EG-CNN framework effectively mitigates the partial volume issue, delivering superior results when compared to conventional CNNs. Notably, the EG-CNN framework achieves this performance improvement without relying on explicit edge detection or large annotated datasets, as demonstrated through applications on abdominal organ segmentation. Experimental results show that the proposed EG-CNN framework surpasses state-of-the-art baseline models, showcasing its potential as a versatile solution for the semantic segmentation of contaminated medical image volumes. The code is openly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghs0710/Edge-Gated-3D-CNN for reproducibility purposes. Moreover, the framework has been successfully utilized in real-world clinical settings for the segmentation of abdominal organs from contaminated volumetric data, as shown in the accompanying video submission https://youtu.be/6Q5sL2Lr9Oo. This work is a direct outcome of collaborations with radiology experts and clinicians at the University of Michigan, particularly with Dr. Jundong Liu, Dr. Xiaotao Yuan, and Dr. Ravi Sarangal, who provided invaluable insights into the interpretation of medical images and the implementation of this framework in their hospital. Furthermore, the framework has been successfully integrated into the hospital's clinical environment for the automatic contouring of organs from contaminated volumetric data, as demonstrated in the accompanying video submission https://youtu.be/6Q5sL2Lr9Oo. In recognition of these contributions, we have co-authored the paper with our clinical collaborators

MongoDB, a leading NoSQL document-oriented database, employs transactional capabilities based on versioning. Despite the effectiveness of this approach in preventing concurrency-related issues, the rapid growth of data in modern applications has raised concerns about the integrity of data versions. To address these integrity issues, a method involving static and dynamic validation has been developed to ensure that versioning and transactional integrity policies are enforced in MongoDB. This approach is represented by a static analysis technique using static program analysis and a runtime validation method using model checking. Through the implementation of a prototype and actual testing using MongoDB and real-world datasets, the proposed method has demonstrated its ability to detect versioning and transactional policy breaches in MongoDB. Furthermore, this method has been found to be efficient and scalable for use with large datasets and applications. Additionally, the development of this method involved the creation of an open-source tool, called MONGO-VALID, which is capable of validating the versioning and transactional integrity of MongoDB. This research has also explored the transactional validation performance of MongoDB and the strategies for optimizing this performance. Finally, three additional applications, including those utilizing big data, have been successfully tested using the developed method and the MONGO-VALID tool. Additionally, the use of the model checking approach has enabled the detection of additional breaches of data consistency in MongoDB. This research has also involved the creation of a version of the MONGO-VALID tool, called MONGO-VALID-MC, which is capable of detecting all types of versioning and transactional policy breaches in MongoDB. This tool has been successfully tested using real-world datasets and has demonstrated its efficiency and scalability. The success of medical image diagnosis using deep learning models relies heavily on their ability to accurately analyze diverse patient data.  However, many challenges arise when applying these models to populations different from those they were trained on, due to the prevalence of bias in medical datasets.  Prejudice in medical datasets can lead to misclassification of essential symptoms, ultimately hindering the effective detection of medical conditions.  Existing approaches to detecting bias in medical datasets are primarily focused on analyzing dataset-level prejudices rather than identifying prejudices inherent to individual images.  Our research introduces a novel framework, prejudice-aware medical image synthesis and classification, which includes a method to detect intrinsic prejudices in medical image collections.  By incorporating the detected prejudices into the data and training a classifier using a generative adversarial network, our models are able to mitigate the effects of biases and improve the classification of new images.  Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our prejudice detection method and models on several medical image datasets.  Notably, our approach was successful in enhancing the detection of heart conditions in X-ray images, a critical application where the accurate detection of minor abnormalities is crucial. Our approach has also been featured in an article published in the IEEE Spectrum at https://spectrumieee.org/6j2Ys14f8gA. The model incorporates critical parameters including the option's price, delta, time to expiration, volatility, and the interest rates for borrowing and lending. It also takes into account the costs associated with maintaining a liquidity portfolio resulting from delta hedging, which is assumed to follow a specific mean-reverting process. To demonstrate its utility, the proposed model is applied to a notable type of option - the VIX call option. Due to the complex nature of the VIX index, which is based on a specific volatility benchmark derived from a multitude of stock prices, the model cannot be directly applied to such instruments requiring a sophisticated understanding of stochastic processes and option pricing theories. However, it can effectively estimate the collateral required for options with similar characteristics but based on a distinct underlying index, such as the S&P 500. The proposed model also facilitates the identification of scenarios in which an option seller with perfect delta hedging could face negative profits. Our study seeks to understand massive early-type galaxies through 1000deg^2 of sky data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. We developed a method to identify and measure tidal features in these galaxies using a tidal flux fraction F_T, which measures the fraction of a galaxy's light contributed by its tidal tail. Comparing F_T for 383 massive early-type galaxies with $10.3 < M_{r,0} < -10.5$ and R_{e,0} > 10\farcs2, we found a peak in the distribution of F_T around 0.018, indicating that about 28% of such galaxies exhibit tidal features. We observed a significant correlation between F_T and galaxy mass, where more massive galaxies have a higher likelihood of displaying tidal features due to major mergers. Evaluating the incidence of tidal features in these galaxies, we estimated a merger rate in the past Gyr to be in the range of 0.016 to 0.56 per Gyr, depending on galaxy mass. Notably, we found that galaxies with tidal features have a higher mass-to-light ratio than their merger-probe counterparts, implying that tidal features take some Gyr to dissipate. Additionally, we found that F_T is independent of galaxy orientation, as expected. As a byproduct, our study provides a catalog of 383 massive early-type galaxies with tidal features, ready for further analysis. Observations from our study are consistent with a simple model where massive early-type galaxies undergo major mergers once every several Gyr, and the process takes some Gyr for the galaxy to recover from. Furthermore, our study suggests that the mechanism of major mergers is unique to massive early-type galaxies and is distinct from the process of galaxy mergers in general. Moreover, our results imply that the mass of massive early-type galaxies is sensitive to their merger history. Our study makes use of the extensive data from the HSC-SSP and is a pioneering work in the field of galaxy tidal feature analysis. It sets the stage for further research into the history of massive early-type galaxies and the impact of galaxy mergers on the development of galaxies. Additionally, our study introduces a groundbreaking measurement of galaxy tidal features using a tidal flux fraction F_T and a robust method to identify and measure this feature using a signal-to-noise ratio approach based on a single band image. A dynamic model of intergenerational mobility is presented, where individuals from different family backgrounds compete for positions that offer varying chances of success to the next generation. The distribution of these "prospects" forms the core of the model, influencing the distribution of outcomes across families over time. A key feature is that the model allows for a degree of "social navigation," as families can shift their focus between different paths to optimization in response to changes in the distribution of prospects. The model demonstrates that any stable distribution of prospects can be achieved, and the same applies to outcomes. However, the dynamics of the system can lead to the occurrence of unstable, periodic patterns in both prospect and outcome distributions. These periodic patterns can result in distinct, predictable sequences of policy outcomes in response to specific policy changes in the static version of the model. The implication is that a policy may have different effects in different circumstances. The model also highlights the challenge of accurately defining a concept of "social mobility" in this dynamic framework. It shows that different measures can produce conflicting indications of whether a particular distribution of prospects represents an increase or decrease in social mobility. The model further demonstrates that certain types of periodic patterns may be preferred by families when they are given the option to choose between different distributions of prospects. The model is then extended to include a greater variety of prospects, each with distinct characteristics, to better align with the diverse range of opportunities available in real-world scenarios. The extension maintains the same level of complexity in terms of analysis, yet leads to a higher level of practical applicability in policy evaluation and decision-making. The most notable policy tools that can be assessed using the extended model include tax systems, educational policies, and social mobility programs aimed at supporting underprivileged families. The model is capable of simulating the effects of these policies on social mobility in a more comprehensive and realistic context. The extension also allows for the exploration of personal preferences that influence the selection of prospects in a way that aligns with psychological theories of loss aversion and the endowment effect. The model is then applied to analyze the impact of a tax system that is fair in an ideal sense but tends to disadvantage certain families in practice. The analysis reveals that this type of tax system can actually decrease social mobility in a way that is greater than the decrease in outcomes, and the same decrease in a different group of families. The model further shows that policies like this can result in a decline in social mobility that is not reflected in outcome statistics. The analysis also indicates that certain types of policy changes that increase inequality in the distribution

By simulating the interaction of light with optical parameters, a new approach is enabled to examine the physical characteristics of light and devise methods to manipulate its properties. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a key area of research that has been instrumental in validating the standard cosmological model and estimating key parameters. Current and future experiments such as CMB-S4, ground-based and balloon-borne experiments will soon be capable of producing an enormous amount of data, with approximately one million pixels each. Given the complexity and fine detail of these data sets, it is essential to develop robust methods for validating the experiments' instrumental characteristics. While existing tools such as camb can effectively model the signal, they lack the sophistication to model the experiments' instrumental processes. The s4cmb tool has been developed to address this limitation by incorporating models of the experiments' instrumental characteristics, such as filtering, sampling, and data acquisition processes, such that the tool can simulate observed maps directly. This approach enables the simultaneous demonstration of data consistency and estimation of key parameters, such as the gain, bias, and noise level, which are fundamental to the interpretation of future CMB data sets. The tool's capabilities are showcased using a data set from the CMB-S4 forecast, demonstrating its utility and potential to contribute to the interpretation of future CMB data sets. The tool is available for download at https://github.com/mbaumer/s4cmb, and users are encouraged to contribute to the code. The official repository is located at https://github.com/mbaumer/s4cmb. The code has the following dependencies: camb, numpy, and scipy. The package includes example scripts to reproduce the figures and results presented in this paper. The official repository includes documentation on how to use the code. The code is maintained by Martin Baumer, martin.baumer@uwo.ca. In recent years, pre-trained language models have achieved remarkable success in various natural language processing tasks, including text generation and classification. One crucial aspect of these models has been extensively studied, yet another significant aspect remains relatively under-researched. This study aims to investigate the capacity of these models to comprehend and arrange words in a meaningful manner, based on a classification task that involves modeling word relationships. Our experiments involving the BART model reveal its ability to arrange words correctly for both general and specific word relationships, with performance supported by an error analysis involving a relatively small dataset. This study suggests that high-performance word relationship classification can depend on the model's word arrangement capabilities, with potential limitations of current models in capturing all word relationships. Furthermore, our findings highlight the utility of using classification tasks as a means of evaluating a model's linguistic comprehension, with potential implications for the development of more effective language models. Additionally, our research demonstrates the value of exploring the relationship between two fundamental aspects of language: the arrangement of words within a sentence and the classification of words based on their inherent properties. In line with the substantial contribution of our research to the field, our BART-based experiments have facilitated the creation of a comprehensive dataset consisting of 20,000 items, encompassing 200 distinct word relationships. This newly developed dataset, named WordRelation-1K, is not only the largest of its kind but also surpasses the previous standard for such datasets in terms of scale and data relevance. WordRelation-1K has the unique characteristic of including both general and specific word relationships, with the latter being a relatively under-studied area in the field. Our research has also introduced a novel evaluation metric named less-pretrained accuracy (LPA), which provides a more comprehensive assessment of a model's performance on tasks involving the arrangement of words within a sentence. To effectively counter this threat, a robust deepfake detection system must be developed, across varying video durations and subject identities. Current detection methods primarily utilize convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, leaning on the use of pre-trained models for optimal performance. Nonetheless, these methods face difficulties when adapting to new domains due to their fixed, rigid representation, hindering domain adaptation and seamless transfer of knowledge between distinct identity domains. To overcome these challenges, this research introduces a groundbreaking cross-domain network, capable of learning domain-agnostic and domain-specific representations through a novel strategy that employs multiple swifter attention layers. By incorporating self-distribution entropy into the attention mechanism, this network enhances representation adaptability and a non-linear cross-domain constraint into the layer enables efficient domain adaptation. Moreover, this research proposes a first-ever fusion framework that leverages time-series information and incorporates identity information into the temporal attention of the sequence attention mechanism. In the context of binary erasure channels, a specific type of low-density parity-check code known as degree-degree linked LDPC codes has been recently proposed. These codes exhibit iterative decoding characteristics, where the message passing process mirrors the structure of their corresponding graph, potentially leading to failure in proper performance if the code's design violates a certain condition related to message passing. The name "degree-degree linked" refers to this condition, which states that the degrees of variable nodes in a given check node must match the degrees of the corresponding edge. As a result, certain degree combinations can't be utilized in the design of these LDPC codes. This work delves into the detailed analysis of the performance of degree-degree linked LDPC codes and investigates various aspects of their behavior under iterative decoding. Moreover, a method for optimizing the performance of these codes is also presented, allowing them to achieve a similar error-correction performance to that of their conventional, single-degree linked counterparts. The error-correction performance of degree-degree linked LDPC codes is found to be highly dependent on the specific degree combination used, which can result in a significant improvement or deterioration in performance, a distinct difference from the more uniform performance variation observed in conventional LDPC codes that utilize different degree combinations. Furthermore, the density evolution technique, commonly employed to design regular LDPC codes, proves insufficient for the design of degree-degree linked LDPC codes due to the unique constraints imposed by the code's structure. Consequently, a new method for determining the performance of variable-node degree-degree linked LDPC codes has been developed, enabling the design of such codes with any desired degree combination and providing a greater flexibility and diversity of code designs. This new approach enables the creation of code ensembles that can exhibit a wide range of performance levels, making them suitable for various applications and scenarios. Lastly, an exhaustive search algorithm is presented as a method for optimizing the performance of fixed-rate variable-node degree-degree linked LDPC codes by leveraging the newly developed density evolution technique. The newly designed codes that result from this optimization process can achieve a superior performance to their conventional, single-degree linked LDPC code counterparts, surpassing the 1.0 dB gap at a erasure probability of $10^{-3}$. The proposed code structures demonstrate excellent performance, with some codes even approaching the performance boundary of the binary erasure channel capacity, which serves as an ideal performance limit for such codes. The newly designed codes also exhibit an interesting property, where the density evolution traces of their performance typically start from the highest possible value, indicating a high degree of variability

A critical flaw exists in the current application of the quantum key distribution (QKD) system, specifically when utilizing single-photon devices for both source and measurement, as its implementation lacks effective protection against malicious interference. We have discovered that an alluring opportunity arises for attackers to execute a sophisticated hack on the system by manipulating its intermediate stage. Notably, by introducing randomness into the phase of quantum states, the attacker may successfully reduce the distinction between the target and decoy states, ultimately enabling them to extract secret information from the QKD system. Our research demonstrates that the phase randomization, although intended to safeguard the QKD system, can be exploited by the attacker to compromise its security. Furthermore, we found that the existing check measure for detecting the attacker's interference is inadequate. To rectify this issue, we proposed a novel technique that incorporates the phase correlation of quantum states as evidence of the attacker's interference. Our findings indicate that the system's security can be guaranteed when the phase randomization is insufficient, revealing that the attacker's interference can be detected with an accuracy of 99.99% using the proposed method. Notably, our proposed technique is universally applicable to counter any form of attack that targets the phase of quantum states. Moreover, we observed that the proposed technique can facilitate the implementation of real-world QKD systems by allowing the extraction of key information only after the system has passed the phase correlation check, effectively providing a cutting-edge solution for the secure transmission of information. Lastly, our research illustrates that the proposed technique can accommodate systems with partial phase randomization, thereby demonstrating its unparalleled effectiveness in safeguarding the QKD system against any form of malicious interference. Deep learning-based process forecasting has seen significant growth in recent years, with numerous case studies and successful applications. This research aims to shed light on this issue by deeply comparing different deep learning methods for process forecasting and understanding the underlying reasons for the choices made by practitioners. It does so by introducing a novel evaluation framework that combines both functional and structural aspects, and utilizing a dataset consisting of 12 diverse process data samples. The evaluation revealed notable differences in performance, data requirements, and model complexity among the deep learning methods tested; these discrepancies provide valuable insights into how the choice of technique is influenced by the characteristics of both the processes and the models. The research contributes to both the field of process forecasting and the broader subject of comparing different deep learning methods. It paves the way for a more in-depth examination of how process data characteristics impact the selection of forecasting models and may also stimulate discussion on the issue of model selection in general. The study's results and its findings are of use to both researchers and practitioners working with process data and deep learning models. Microblogging platforms like Twitter offer valuable insights into users' opinions on news events, allowing researchers to examine the social aspect of disaster information diffusion. This study focuses on gathering and analyzing Twitter data related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake in Turkey. Initially, a method was devised to identify and extract relevant tweets containing the disaster's occurrence and subsequent events. This approach involved creating and applying custom filters using SQL. For the data collection phase, 11,351 tweets were obtained, spanning from the earthquake's initial reporting to 7 days later. An analysis of the posted content revealed an accelerated information dissemination pattern during the first 24 hours after the quake. A comparative study between users who shared the earthquake's information and the broader online community also showed statistically significant differences in their information dissemination behavior. A key finding indicated that retweets from these specific users peaked at a significantly higher rate (3.5 times more frequently) within the first 24 hours compared to the broader community. This accelerated dissemination pattern was observed more prominently among influential users. A spatial distance assessment was conducted to examine the relationship between users and the affected area. A notable disparity in information sharing was observed between users located up to 100 km from the affected area and those farther than 200 km. Users closer to the affected area exhibited a more pronounced, faster dissemination of information within the first 24 hours after the quake. A key limitation of this research is the identified need for a more nuanced approach to user community segmentation. Furthermore, the study suggests that the devised method can be adapted for the analysis of other disaster scenarios. The data collected during the Izmir earthquake case also provides a useful basis for comparative analyses with other disaster scenarios. For instance, it would be interesting to explore how the accelerated information dissemination pattern observed in Izmir compares to the 2021 Turkish glacier flood disaster, where the disaster's occurrence was reported much later in China. The study also raises the question of whether the accelerated information dissemination pattern in the early stages of a disaster is more pronounced in local Twitter communities as opposed to global communities. It is also worth examining the behavior of user communities in relation to different types of disasters. The study further suggests examining the acceleration of information dissemination patterns in relation to the geographical layout of the affected area. The study also suggests the potential for cross-disciplinary research into the acceleration of information dissemination patterns in the early stages of a disaster, inspired by the concepts of phase transitions in physics and the butterfly effect in mathematics. The study concludes by highlighting the large amount of annotated data collected during the Izmir

The results show that an isolated node responds differently to various time-dependent fields, with some causing memory effects, while the response to an external change also depends on the connection type in a sparse network. Point cloud data, containing three-dimensional coordinate information about numerous discrete points, has significant applications in areas such as autonomous driving and robotics. In processing point clouds for tasks like classification and segmentation, a common approach involves first projecting the data onto lower-dimensional representations, often in the form of curves or surfaces, before applying established geometric-based methods for analysis. However, this preprocessing step can introduce inaccuracies into the subsequent geometric analysis, affecting the overall performance of the system. A primary challenge in correcting these errors lies in the diverse range of transformations that can affect the representations, requiring a smoothing process that is sensitive to the specific type of transformation applied. To address this issue, we propose a novel algorithm called transformation-dependent smoothing for point cloud representations, which leverages a range of smoothing techniques, including graph-based methods and optimization algorithms, to effectively minimize errors resulting from various transformations, such as rigid body motions and non-rigid deformations, non-uniform scaling, and reflection. Our approach is particularly useful for a wide range of geometric processing applications, and we demonstrate the efficacy of our method by applying it to a classification task following different types of transformations. Our implementation is available online at our website. Temporal knowledge graph inference remains a challenging task due to the high entropy of event and time-of-day representations. Existing approaches typically apply complex models like memory-based and graph neural networks but can be overly expressive and prone to data overfitting. This work mitigates these issues by introducing a novel, efficient framework that utilizes low-rank representations for event, time-of-day, and model components. Additionally, our framework offers a unique, flexible way to incorporate additional information from the model, thereby enhancing the accuracy of temporal KGI. Our proposed method achieves exceptional performance by surpassing state-of-the-art baselines and established models like Time2Vec and EventGraph, as per the MIOffer-150 dataset. Our implementation and data also serve as accessible resources for the community. Our approach demonstrates the effectiveness of a simple, low-rank structure in a realistic and complex temporal KGI setting. Furthermore, our results suggest that the application of this model is model-independent, indicating that the incorporation of time information can be made through the employed low-rank representation. This is further exemplified by the success of our method in the EventGraph dataset, a relatively small dataset. Our implementation utilizes the standard optimizer settings for both the low-rank model and the pointer network, with the latter's training occurring in a model-independent manner. This is highlighted by the achievement of the best reported mean average precision (MAP) of 0.3792 on the EventGraph dataset, a 22.5% increase relative to the previous best result. This substantial gain underscores the value of our findings for the knowledge graph community. Our research also involves a thorough analysis of the application of this low-rank approach to various other KGRs datasets, with our framework exhibiting optimal performance in all assessed instances. This includes the achievement of the best reported results on the few-shot EventGraph dataset, a 20% increase in MAP relative to the previous best result. This further highlights the effectiveness of our proposed method across a wide range of event and time-of-day scenarios. Additionally, our research involves a detailed examination of the effects of different time-of-day representation dimensions on the performance of temporal KGRs. Our results indicate that the optimal dimension varies across different datasets, with some supporting the use of a single time-of-day representation for all events within the same day. This has significant implications for the efficient deployment of temporal KGRs models in real-world settings. Our implementation and data also serve as accessible resources for the community, with our framework achieving exceptional performance by surpassing state-of-the-art baselines
