In recent years, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have experienced remarkable success in generating complex textual data. Current GAN-based text generation models predominantly utilize a single opponent model to refine the generator's output, which leads to several limitations: the opponent model's complexity is not optimized, the generated text does not effectively reflect the opponent's perspective, and the training process is not fully optimized. To address these challenges, this paper introduces SparseGAN, an innovative framework that mitigates these issues by incorporating the following key components: a minimal set of trained discriminator models, each representing a opponent network with distinct parameters; a generator that synthesizes text with the perspective of these opponent networks in unison. By incorporating multiple opponent networks, the generated text exhibits enhanced coherence and quality. Furthermore, the training of the generator and opponent networks is facilitated through a dual-objective adversarial learning approach, which enables end-to-end optimization. The experimental evaluations on the Gigaword Dataset reveal that the proposed SparseGAN outperforms the state-of-the-art sequence generation models, including transformer-based models, in terms of the perceived naturalness and coherence of the generated text. By examining the contents of comets and meteorites, scientists can gather clues about the spread of life throughout the solar system and across vast distances. While microbial life has been suggested to have existed for an estimated 3.5 billion to 4.0 billion years, the difficulty lies in determining whether life was transferred through interstellar means or emerged independently in each given time frame. To better understand this phenomenon, the focus should be on earth's surroundings during that time period, rather than all possible sources of the sky. In the context of an undirected connected graph G, a k-edge independent st-path is a path connecting nodes s and t, utilizing no more than k edges that other paths between s and t also do not utilize. The objective of this project is to accurately calculate within a factor of $\lambda$ greater than the true value, the total number of edges in all k-edge independent st-paths in a given graph. It has previously been established that both fixed and variable k edge independent st-paths in general graphs can be identified with a time complexity of O(k^3*\log k) and O(k^2*\log k) respectively. This study introduces a non-approximable k for certain types of graphs, indicating the impossibility of accurately calculating the minimum edge weight of independent st-paths when k is sufficiently large. Furthermore, this study proposes an accurate calculation of minimum edge weight for 2-edge independent st-paths in O(\sqrt k) time complexity, as well as for certain types of graphs, including trees, planar graphs, and cubic graphs, but does not provide a specific time complexity for these types of graphs. Additionally, this study proposes a general algorithm for accurately calculating minimum edge weight for k-edge independent st-paths in O(k^{3/2}*log k) time complexity. This algorithm is further analyzed on the mentioned types of graphs, and it is demonstrated that its time complexity matches the required time complexity for these types of graphs, indicating that the proposed algorithm achieves the best possible time complexity for these types of graphs. A previous result indicating that any accurate calculation algorithm for edge weight must utilize a space complexity of at least k is utilized to prove that a similar time and space complexity restriction applies to the calculation of minimum edge weight for k-edge independent st-paths. Furthermore, this study proposes an accurate calculation of minimum edge weight for k-edge independent st-paths in a graph G by reducing the calculation of minimum edge weight in graph G to the calculation of a specific property in a transformed graph G', and transforming back the result to obtain the final answer. This is achieved by introducing a family of supermodular functions that can be utilized to reduce the calculation of minimum edge weight in graph G to the calculation of a specific property in graph G', and utilizing the properties of supermodular functions to prove the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of an optimal solution under certain constraints. To address this, researchers have developed various methods to measure structural polarization within interconnected online networks, aiming to objectiveely assess polarization. While utilizing conformal theories for complex gravitational systems has been successful, a lack of a consistent Hamiltonian formulation for general relativity within the conformal thin-slice approach has hindered its application in numerical relativity. This study rectifies this shortcoming by formulating an effective stress tensor for the conformal metric resulting from the Conformal Thin-Shell Transition (CTTK). In turn, this enables the incorporation of numerous matter fields, including both barotropic fluids and Polytrope stars, within the context of numerical relativity. In an accompanying paper, we demonstrate the utility of CTTK in numerical relativity for the specific case of polytropic stars. Here, we delve into the technical details behind deriving the stress tensor of the conformal metric due to the shell, including deriving Hamiltonian dynamics for the conformal metric and matter fields, and an associated Hamiltonian boundary term. We also outline the steps for implementing CTTK within Numerical Relativity Codes. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our formulation on the choice of gauge and the development of an appropriate boundary condition for the conformal metric and its derivatives in the CTTK framework. This includes introducing a novel "Conformal Thin-Shell Transition" gauge, along with a corresponding modification to the boundary value problem, which results in a more robust and stable numerical implementation of CTTK. Ultimately, our approach offers a flexible and adaptable framework for incorporating a wide range of matter fields and other field theories within the context of numerical relativity. This is particularly significant, as the development of accurate and reliable numerical relativity codes will be crucial for a next-generation gravitational wave detector like eLISA, given the dense field configurations that such detectors are optimized to detect. This, in turn, will be essential for generating reliable predictions of gravitational wave signals in future experiments. Furthermore, our formulation also provides valuable physical insights into the nature and properties of the shell transition, and given its computational advantages, it has the potential to become the industry standard for numerical relativity codes in the future. Classical logic's bivalency, which posits that every statement is true or false, has been the underlying logic for set theory since the time of Zermelo and Fraenkel. They achieved notable success with this approach, obtaining an intuitive and operationally effective theory as a result. Nevertheless, the bivalency of classical logic is contradicted by the phenomenon of semantic paradoxes, leading to the development of paraconsistent and paracomplete approaches to logic. These approaches relax the bivalency requirement, allowing statements to have a truth value of neither true nor false, or both true and false. The authors of this paper investigate the possibility of incorporating such non-bivalent reasoning into set theory by proposing a variant of Zermelo-Fraenkel logic, referred to as PKFR. In this proposed logic, the law of excluded middle and the law of non-contradiction are no longer universally applicable, instead holding only when justified by a consistent and coherent argument. As a result, statements with non-bivalent truth values can be asserted within PKFR. Moreover, theorems in PKFR demonstrate a key property of consistency, known as the law of conservation, which ensures that the truth of a statement does not depend on its form but rather its underlying content. The law of non-contradiction, although weakened in PKFR, continues to guarantee the impossibility of a statement being both true and false at the same time. The possibility of a paraconsistent set to contain both a member and its complement is allowed in PKFR, albeit with the restriction that such a set's elements must be mutually incompatible. The authors also introduce a rule for interpreting the law of excluded middle in a way that is analogous to the rule for the law of non-contradiction, allowing for the expression of classical truths within PKFR using intensional set operators. The resulting PKFR is found to be as effective as the classical Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory in addressing the semantic paradoxes and other challenges. The paper concludes by outlining the possibilities for further exploration in the realm of constructive mathematics using PKFR. The name PKFR is used as a shorthand for the logic that includes the principles of paraconsistency, parocompleteness, the law of non-contradiction, the law of excluded middle, and the law of conservation. The authors propose the term 'positive logic' to encompass not only PKFR but also other logics that share its core characteristics. The name 'constructive logic' is already in use

Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling the incorporation of reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination into phylogenetic analysis. In contrast to the numerous computational tools available for constructing phylogenetic trees, a relatively limited number of methods have been developed for generating phylogenetic networks while accounting for reticulate evolutionary processes. A systematic comparison of the underlying principles and applications of these phylogenetic network creation methods has not been conducted previously. This detection system was tested on a type of fish cells and compared to a traditional tracking approach, revealing that it is more resilient to variations in the size of cells and more accurate in predicting future cell movements. Furthermore, it was found that cell movements can be distinguished from other movements based on speed and persistence, allowing for the identification of cells that are engaged in meaningful activities. Additionally, it was observed that cells within certain areas of the tissue exhibit distinct movement patterns. Our research involves utilizing the Weil restriction to derive an isogeny between genus-1 curves and genus-3 superelliptic curves, where the 3-torsion point is linked to a rational point on the genus-1 curve. Building upon this connection, we establish an association between genus-3 superellic curves and genus-1 curves through the medium of 3-descent on genus-1 curves, which provides the basis for our final conclusion: a genus-3 superelliptic curve has a non-holomorphic three-torsion point if, and only if, its associated genus-1 curve has a non-holomorphic two-torsion point collectible via Weil restriction from a quadratic field. Our most notable contribution involves demonstrating the existence of a vast family of genus-3 superelliptic curves possessing non-holomorphic three-torsion points, which includes curves with potentially large prime factors in their j-invariant values, which can be used as a component in the 3-descent method for their associated genus-1 curves. This specifically refers to curves of genus-3 with the characteristic of having a non-holomorphic three-torsion point, whose associated genus-1 curves require at least six descents to determine the factorization of their Jacobian. This achievement is made possible by our unique approach, which leverages the use of Weil restrictions in the context of the 3-descent method, an aspect that has not been employed in previous studies. Although these models provide the degree of connection between variables, the accuracy of the linear predictions within the model is not automatically guaranteed. We investigated whether strong connections in a graph implied linear relationships between the corresponding variables. Assuming a well-conditioned model, we found the formula for the implied variance of a variable given the connections from its predecessors. Based on this, we created a method to determine the degree of linearity, which can be applied even if the original assumptions are not met. This method is independent of any specific estimation procedure and can be used to validate the linear assumptions within network autoregressive models. Through simulated data, we demonstrated that this approach enhances the performance compared to alternative methods. Furthermore, we applied this evaluation method to real-world electricity consumption networks and found non-linear interactions in certain areas of these networks. The implementation of this evaluation method is provided in the form of an available Python package called LinearityChecker. Distributed applications relying on cloud environments for computation often experience significant performance fluctuations when synchronizing processes due to the underlying virtual machine (VM) communication system's varying efficiency. Although such variations are supposed to be minimized by the vendor-provided virtualization layer, our research reveals that the impact of this'sound in the clouds' should not be underestimated, particularly for applications with poor synchronization. We demonstrate through theoretical analysis and real-world testing on a OpenStack-based test bed that the effects of communication system variability can result in decreased scalability for certain workloads. Moreover, we observe that the performance consequences are more pronounced when using smaller VMs. In an effort to mitigate these performance fluctuations and improve the consistency of communication system variability, we propose assigning a fixed amount of VMs for each-thread applications to align VM boundaries with application boundaries. By doing so, we successfully increase the scalability of our test applications by three to five times when using smaller VMs. This research provides a fundamental understanding of the performance fluctuations experienced by distributed applications in cloud environments and presents a straightforward yet effective solution for enhancing the scalability of such workloads. In large-scale systems with numerous learning agents, it is often impractical for the agents to share their settings with a central controller due to privacy concerns and the vastness of the action space. In such scenarios, it is beneficial to design decentralized schemes that allow agents to share their observations with the controller, thereby facilitating the development of optimal policies while maintaining confidentiality. This paper introduces a first-ever communication-efficient scheme for learning in situational linear bandits, where the controller utilizes historical observations from individual agents, along with their shared feedback, to derive a linear approximation of the agents' context. By leveraging this context through a variational autoencoder, the controller formulates an estimated context for each agent and identifies an optimal action through linear optimization. The proposed scheme involves linear optimization, estimated context update, and a distributed Situational Linearize Learning (SILL) algorithm that incorporates both batch and online variants. Theoretical analysis for a constant reward model reveals that the estimated context yields a suboptimal but achievable reward, thereby facilitating the derivation of a sublinear regret bound for the SILL algorithm. The results demonstrate the practical efficacy of the scheme through numerical experiments and highlight its potential to handle massive action spaces. The scheme is further applicable to general linear contextual bandits, presenting a sublinear regret bound for a time-dependent reward model. The SILL algorithm is particularly suited for a significant class of wireless sensor applications, wherein the controller is typically represented as a fusion center with a limited number of connections to individual agents. The proposed scheme yields a sublinear regret bound for these settings, with a specific parameter configuration demonstrating a regret performance an order of magnitude better than existing solutions. The SILL algorithm further extends the distributed linear contextual bandits algorithm (DiLinCB) through a more complex context formulation, resulting in a more complex optimization problem that yields a sublinear regret bound for a time-dependent reward model. The paper's contributions are showcased through an energy harvesting application, highlighting the potential of the proposed scheme to handle massive action spaces, providing a first-ever communication-efficient solution for learning in situational linear bandits. The scheme's efficacy is further validated through an analysis of the proposed SILL algorithm's regret performance, its efficient communication requirements, and its distributional benefits for wireless sensor applications. The paper's results demonstrate the potential of communication-efficient decentralized learning for optimizing the performance of complex systems with numerous learning agents. The proposed SILL algorithm yields a sublinear regret bound for a time-dependent reward model, with a parameter configuration that provides an order of magnitude better regret performance than existing solutions.

A significant issue in developing autonomous robots for exploration is addressing the challenge of unpredictable terrain. In this project, a simplified mechanical model of a one-legged hopping robot was developed, considering the effects of deformable terrain. By assuming a linear elastic terrain response, the model includes the interaction between the robot and the environment. A key feature of the model is the presence of a periodic motion phase when the foot is lifted off the ground, characterized by harmonic oscillations resulting from the elastic terrain's response. This periodic component causes variations in the ground reaction force, leading to increased energy transfer between the robot and the terrain. To minimize these variations and optimize the robot's performance, a control method was implemented using active control of the robot's movements during the ground contact phase. The implementation of this control method was found to lead to a reduction in motion asymmetry and energy exchange between the robot and the terrain. In addition, the model was used to investigate the effects of changing the robot's design, terrain stiffness, and the size of the foot on the robot's movement and energy transfer. The findings of this study can inform the design of one-legged robots to optimize their performance on yielding terrain. We demonstrate that solutions near equilibrium will inevitably exhibit oscillatory behavior in their Fourier transform, driven by an exponentially growing component aligned with the direction of the force. This phenomenon leads to an increased diffusion rate in the energy space. Additionally, we identify a specific frequency range where the oscillatory frequencies are optimized, resulting in an enhanced diffusion rate that is determined by the force's first derivative rather than a second order term. Unfortunately, this optimized diffusion rate is not sufficient to ensure the non-polarized phase-blending hypothesis, which would imply a distinct energy split in the Fourier transform of solutions. Counterexamples exist, illustrating that the required condition of a positive second-order derivative along the direction of the force does not guarantee the hypothesized sharper energy decay rate. These conclusions hold without restriction on the angle of incidence. Moreover, our findings remain valid in any dimension greater than one. The methods employed in this study involve a detailed analysis of the linearized Boltzmann equation and its associated semi-group of collisions, characterized by a strongly continuous mapping from the space of bounded functions to itself. We establish the existence, continuity, and differentiability of this semi-group, along with its adjoint, and derive their respective spectra using a Fourier transform approach. We also identify a key relationship between the spectrum of the semi-group and the fundamental solution of the linearized Boltzmann equation. The analysis of the semi-group's spectrum allows us to determine the optimized frequency component and the associated Taylor diffusion rate. Conversely, this optimized frequency component may be interpreted as the highest derivative of the solution's mapping that is continuous with respect to its initial conditions. We demonstrate that the optimized frequency component satisfies a specific equation, providing a general framework for the phenomenon of Taylor diffusion in linear equations. This framework is applicable not only to the one-force case within the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation but also to a broader class of linear equations, including but not limited to the radiation transport equation and the quantum harmonic oscillator equation. However, determining the accuracy of these methods near coastal areas is challenging due to a lack of suitable observations. By utilizing high-frequency observations of the upwelling radiation from the top layer of the ocean, obtained through the Spatio-spectral imaging experiment on board the Metop-B satellite, we conducted a study in the Baltic Sea. We found that a specific wave-crest parameter, related to the fourth moment of the sea surface slope, to be more resistant to changes caused by wind direction than other wave-crest statistics. This preferred parameter exhibited a relatively slow variation when modeled using a linear function of tan^-1, with a time-scale of approximately one day, indicating that it retains important information about wave morphology while minimizing the effect of wind direction. We also observed that by using this parameter in models of upwelling radiation, we could account for the effects of wind direction, and in doing so, we significantly reduced the error when comparing the modeled values to actual measured values of upwelling radiation, obtained through the Infrared Atmospheric Sounding Interferometer on board the Metop-B satellite, across a range of sea conditions. Furthermore, we found that using the same model but with a higher frequency observation of upwelling radiation as input, resulted in a lower root mean square error. We were able to achieve the lowest rmse of all methods for determining ocean wave roughness, a key parameter for modeling the interaction between solar radiation and the ocean, when using a combination of the wave-crest parameter and the angular second moment of the sea surface slope. This method yielded a significantly lower rms than all other methods, including traditional approaches based on wind speed alone. Additionally, we discovered that this method could accurately estimate ocean wave roughness even in coastal areas, without the need for any additional adjustments, and with a much lower error than methods that rely on wind speed alone, which can vary significantly over short distances in these areas. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread consequences and collected digital data that can be utilized for healthcare system monitoring via social media. To effectively utilize such data, a dataset labeled with the emotions expressed within microblogging posts during the pandemic is crucial. However, gathering labeled data is challenging due to the diverse nature of opinions presented in social media platforms. In this research, a dataset comprising of COVID-19 related emotions within microblogging posts was created through a crowdsourcing approach, where 3,824 posts were collected from Twitter and labeled by 12 individuals who annotated the posts with their perceived emotional content using a self-assessment manikin (SAM) technique. The resulting dataset comprises of 4,792 posts annotated with one of the four emotions: happiness, sadness, fear, and disgust. To validate the constructed dataset, a series of experiments were conducted to assess the classification accuracy of existing machine learning models. The findings of these experiments highlighted the importance of considering contextual information within the posts, in addition to the extracted features, for accurate classification. Furthermore, the implementation of contextual reasoning within the models resulted in a significant improvement in their performance. The constructed dataset, along with the obtained results, can benefit researchers in the field of affective computing and text classification. The collected data and annotation guidelines are made available for the research community to facilitate further exploration and development of more sophisticated classification approaches. The utilized classification techniques, data preprocessing methods, and annotation guidelines are unique and distinct from the commonly applied strategies. The effectiveness of the proposed approaches was validated through a series of experiments, and the implemented designs have shown potential in enhancing the performance of emotion-related classification tasks. The achieved results demonstrate the capability of neural network-based models to accurately identify the emotional content of posts that are negatively oriented, while slightly less accurate in classifying positively worded posts. The slight deficiency in classification accuracy for positively worded posts is deemed acceptable, given the higher difficulty in differentiating between the four expressed emotions within such posts. The relatively high level of annotator agreement, combined with the relatively low confusion matrix values, adds credibility to the constructed dataset. The obtained results also highlight the importance of considering the context within the posts, a concept that is integral to the realm of affective computing. The implementation of contextual reasoning within the models resulted in a significant improvement in their performance, a finding that is expected to guide the development of future machine learning-based approaches. The unique design and composition of the constructed dataset makes it an attractive platform for testing the performance of machine learning models in a real-world setting

Layer-by-layer conduction measurement, a potent tool, offers a direct means to assess the conduction properties of individual layers in layered materials, albeit with certain limitations such as high applied voltages and potential interlayer connections. Due to these constraints, a straightforward approach to determine whether interlayer connections are serial or parallel is not feasible. As a result, different methods have been employed to analyze layer-by-layer conduction, including resistivity, magnetopetia, and anisotropic transport. Nonetheless, a universal method is still needed to fully comprehend the behavior of layered systems. One commonly adopted method involves analyzing the variation in interlayer resistance in response to an applied electric field. By utilizing this approach, researchers have reported the existence of non-linear behavior in YBa2Cu3O6.75, a type of cuprate that exhibits charge density oscillations, at both temperatures below and above the superconducting transition temperature. A new theoretical model has been developed to explain these observations through the concept of parallel interlayer connections. Although the model demonstrates a non-linear relationship, it requires an assumption that the contact resistance between layers exceeds the layer resistance. In contrast, a different analysis of the data via a function representing the sum of two parallel resistors yields a linear component that aligns with the layer resistance in YBa2Cu3O6.75, thus validating the layer resistance value obtained from magnetopetia measurements. Furthermore, the model also facilitates an estimation of the "barrier height" in YBa2Cu3O6.75, a value that indicates the resistance associated with crossing the interlayer barrier. Additionally, by comparing the "barrier height" in YBa2Cu3O6.75 and Bi2Sr2Ca1-xHaxCu3O10+x, it is revealed that the former exhibits a higher resistance in both normal and superconducting states. A new model has been proposed to explain the non-linear behavior in YBa2Cu3O6.75 through the concept of parallel interlayer connections, with the possibility of implementing a similar model for other layered systems that exhibit non-linear behavior in response to an applied electric field. Nonetheless, a thorough understanding of the underlying physics is necessary to apply this model, such as the effects of an applied electric field on the spatial variation of the superconducting order parameter in YBa2Cu3O6.75. The characteristics of dense hadronic matter within the density range relevant to neutron stars, particularly when strange quarks are present, are not well defined and require further investigation. In this research, we create a complex equation of state for dense hadronic matter by incorporating strange quark fields and examine how it affects the sound speed of this matter as the density changes. Our findings indicate that the sound speed of strange quark matter is higher than that of hadronic matter at similar densities, with an average increase of approximately 10%. This difference in sound speeds has significant implications for the gravitational wave signals produced by binary neutron star mergers. In cases where the stars' interiors comprise dense hadronic matter, the gravitational wave signal will exhibit a larger amplitude and a more pronounced harmonic structure than in scenarios where strange quarks are present. Our research also reveals that a larger fraction of the star's mass density is indicative of a larger sound speed, which in turn results in a greater amplitude and a more pronounced harmonic structure in the gravitational wave signal. Furthermore, the relation between sound speed and adiabatic index is not constant across the density range of neutron stars, which may impact their stability. This index is generally greater than 3/2 and exhibits a significant change as the density increases, posing a challenge for oscillations in neutron stars. In contrast, the gravitational vector perturbations of quark stars with strange quarks at their cores yield frequencies of quasi-normal modes that are consistent with predictions made before the discovery of GW170817, with a minimum frequency of approximately 1.7 kHz. This research also provides a framework for constructing compact stars composed of dense hadronic and strange quark matter models, which can be tested using future observations of the electromagnetic counterparts of neutron star mergers. The onset of phase transitions within these stars, resulting in the formation of distinct phases of hadronic and quark matter, causes a significant delay in the emergence of gravitational wave signals following merger events. This delay, which could range from as short as 10 milliseconds to as long as 30 milliseconds, leaves a distinctive imprint on the accompanying electromagnetic radiation. In contrast, the emission of gravitational waves through neutron star mergers that do not involve phase transitions will not exhibit a notable delay. Furthermore, the sound speed of hadronic matter in neutron stars can be determined from the analysis of electromagnetic counterparts that exhibit a significant delay, with an estimated uncertainty of approximately 0.05. In the future, the detection of multiple neutron star mergers will allow for the calculation of the average sound speed

A commonly adopted strategy to circumvent this limitation is the use of global pooling layers, which compress feature maps into scalar values representing the global characteristic. In our research, we introduce a novel approach to global feature extraction, where we treat pooling operations as part of an optimization process and propose a method to dynamically determine pooling regions through a global mean pooling layer. Our dynamic pooling approach surpasses the standard global pooling layer and achieves comparable performance to spatial pooling layers while being highly computationally efficient. We apply this technique across multiple datasets with remarkable results, demonstrating its versatility and efficacy. Our implementation and data, including our code at https://github.com/zhm-sj/GlobalMeanPoolingLayer, are freely accessible for replication purposes. We have found existing techniques such as SIMC to have limitations in their security assumptions. This study presents a new framework, SIMC 2.0, capable of safeguarding neural network training even if the adversary has control over the client's hardware. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SIMC 2.0 by incorporating it into an end-to-end encrypted neural network communication protocol, without compromising the accuracy of the inferred models. Our findings show that models trained with SIMC 2.0 achieve only a 0.02% decrease in accuracy, compared to standard training, across a range of image and sound classification tasks. Furthermore, the increased computational requirements of SIMC 2.0 are mitigated by its support for model updates using both batch and point estimates. Our implementation of SIMC 2.0 reveals that using point estimates results in a 5 times performance improvement. This enhanced protocol holds significant potential for the secure training of neural networks. Additionally, we propose a new definition for privacy in neural network training, focusing on preventing the disclosure of sensitive information through input data. This definition gives rise to an novel challenge, addressed by our solution, an encryption-based approach for secure training without compromising model accuracy. Our results highlight the feasibility of conducting secure training with reduced reliance on stringent security assumptions, thereby making it more practical and achievable. Furthermore, our proposed definition and solution highlight the intricacies involved in achieving optimal accuracy from models trained in an insecure environment. Our implementation has demonstrated the efficacy of SIMC 2.0, although further research is required to fully explore its applications across all domains of neural network training. Our scheme has raised an intriguing question on achieving optimal accuracy from models trained in an insecure environment, giving rise to a new challenge that our solution has addressed through an encryption-based approach, leading to a new benchmark for all subsequent research in this domain. Our findings have created an opportunity for further exploration into this domain, with our solution serving as a starting point for the development of more sophisticated techniques that can securely train models with greater complexity and larger datasets. By gradually refining the understanding of the question and the underlying graph structure, this approach aims to consolidate the insights gained from the knowledge base, thus enhancing the accuracy of the response. Although mental health services within the criminal justice system are deemed essential, there is a notable lack of empirical research on the psychological well-being of individuals within this system, particularly concerning the effectiveness of compulsory therapy. This study's findings also highlight the need for future research to investigate the specific program components that are associated with improved psychological well-being and lower recidivism rates, as well as the potential benefits of implementing therapy programs within the criminal justice system on a broader scale. We investigated whether a basic consistency regularization technique, combining two distinct strategies, would enhance the performance of deep learning models in image segmentation. The first strategy involves adding label noise, a practice that is an essential component of data augmentation, and the second strategy involves implementing batch normalization, a technique that has a direct connection to consistency regularization. Our research revealed that this basic technique consistently compares favorably to cutting-edge methods and a number of strong baselines in multiple datasets. The code is publicly available on https://github.com/zhm-sj/CRSS. The model we used is a variant of the UNet architecture known as the Double Deep UNet, characterized by two distinct decoding pathways. Two main components contribute to the regularizer of the model: a consistency term and a batch normalization term. The consistency term is responsible for regulating the ambiguity of the model, and the batch normalization term helps to regularize the model by reducing the intra-batch variability. We utilized three distinct strategies for data augmentation in our research, specifically applying random flipping, random rotation, and the construction of an adversarial batch. The model we used is capable of being trained end-to-end. We conducted extensive research in two leading healthcare image segmentation datasets, and the model we used consistently outperformed multiple strong baselines and state-of-the-art methods. The name "awkwardly basic" refers to the fact that deep learning experts may consider the model we used awkward due to its simplicity, and the fact that the name "CRSS" is an abbreviation of "Consistency Regularization for Semi-Supervised Segmentation". The model we used is overparameterized, and the label noise is a core component of data augmentation with a long history dating back to the early stages of deep learning. The term "semi-supervised" is an accurate description of the model we used, as the model we used uses a small number of labeled images in conjunction with a large number of synthetic data through transformations. The model we used is unique in its use of the double deep UNet architecture, the consistency regularization technique, and the construction of an adversarial batch. The model we used is an overparameterized model with a history of performance excellence in multiple datasets.

The ATLAS jet calorimeter trigger system, relying on the decision of the Level-1 trigger system, undergoes a second level of refinement where individual jet objects are examined and their properties are cross-checked against predetermined criteria. The system's architecture is designed such that a single hardware decision can result in substantial system resource utilization, leading to potential bottlenecks. To mitigate this issue, the implementation of the Level-2 jet calorimeter trigger using an ATLAS custom-made ASIC called the CALO Trigger Concentrator (CTC), in conjunction with the Ultrascale+ FPGAs on the ATLAS Trigger Board AT201, allows for adjustable jet finding capabilities. Furthermore, the integration of an CTC chip on the AT201 derivative board, known as the AT201-C, or also referred to as the ATFB2, within the Level-2 jet finder component, is set to provide a solution to the anticipated data throughput challenges on the ATLAS Level-2 trigger system. The AT201-C board variant incorporates two 6Gb/s S360 UltraScale+ FPGAs as its core components. With a total of 192 CTCs integrated onto these FPGAs, the system is capable of processing up to 1 Tbps of data. In addition, the board features a 32-bit 1.6 GHz CPU, a 2 GB on-board memory, as well as two on-board memory modules with 4 GB each, enabling the implementation of the full Level-2 jet finder software. The integrated CPU and memory allows for the management of the data handling, configuration, and the transfer of results to the ATLAS Global Trigger Manager. Moreover, the board also utilizes the ATLAS custom-made 10GbE switch module, known as the ATLAS Trigger Networking System (ATLAS-TNS), for the communication with other Level-2 and the Global Trigger Manager layers. The fully integrated AT201-C board has successfully undergone the necessary testing to validate its performance and functionality prior to its installation in the ATLAS detector during the Extended Shutdown period of the Large Hadron Collider, scheduled to take place in 2021. The LHC is expected to operate at a higher luminosity of 3x10^35 cm^-2s^-1 following the shutdown, resulting in a significant increase in the number of particle collisions during its next phase of operation. As a result, the upgraded AT201-C board will be necessary to effectively handle the higher data throughput resulting from the more frequent collisions. This approach not only enhances the efficiency of quantum simulation but also provides a clear graphical representation of a system's chaotic behavior. By analyzing the evolving graph, we can identify the underlying reasons for a system's disorder, even if only at a semi-analytical level. Using the example of Dirac's equation, we demonstrate how our approach can handle fundamental, relativistic phenomena and the complex interactions that arise from mass-imbalanced mixtures of fermions. Furthermore, our framework is versatile and can be applied to various quantum scenarios, including number conservation and unitary transformations. Due to the involvement of non-local inductive neural processes, our model is capable of capturing long-range, intricate, and real-time interactions between quantum particles. Knowledge tracing has emerged as a leading technology in adapting educational systems to the needs of individual students. A key factor contributing to the success of these systems lies in their ability to accurately predict student knowledge based on their actions within the system. In recent years, deep learning-based approaches have demonstrated remarkable prowess in this prediction aspect, with many incorporating graphical models to leverage the structural connections between skills. Despite the availability of pre-trained models for both graph neural networks and Bayesian networks, a comprehensive evaluation framework is lacking for these knowledge tracing systems. To address this gap, we present pyKT, a novel evaluation toolkit designed to assess the performance of deep learning-based knowledge tracing systems incorporating graphical models. pyKT encompasses a range of metrics, including prediction accuracy and visualization tools, and enables straightforward model ensemble methods and visualization of attention mechanisms. With its user-friendly interface and comprehensive features, pyKT serves as an essential resource for both researchers and practitioners to create, evaluate, and compare various knowledge tracing systems. Furthermore, pyKT is hosted on GitHub, providing an easy-to-use template for submitting evaluation results to the NIPS 2019 Learning on Graphs Workshop Paper Repository. With its open-source and community-driven approach, pyKT is positioned to become a leading evaluation toolkit for both graph machine learning and knowledge tracing communities. Additionally, pyKT has inspired the creation of the KT-Benchmark GitHub repository, a dedicated platform for sharing knowledge tracing datasets, models, and implementation challenges. Leveraging open-source models and a cloud-based evaluation framework, users can easily utilize pyKT for both model development and evaluation. With its flexible architecture, pyKT is easily extensible for both new model support and custom evaluation configurations. In line with its community-driven vision, pyKT is looking for additional contributors to enhance its feature set and model support. For potential contributors, we recommend visiting the pyKT GitHub repository for more information on available features and model support. Similarly, the KT-Benchmark GitHub repository provides details on available datasets, models, and implementation challenges for knowledge tracing. Both pyKT and the KT-Benchmark repository are actively maintained and are seeking additional input from both graph machine learning and knowledge tracing communities. In conclusion, pyKT has established a new standard for the evaluation of deep learning-based knowledge tracing systems, incorporating graphical models. With its comprehensive evaluation metrics, effortless model ensemble methods, and visualization tools, pyKT is the go-to evaluation toolkit for both researchers and practitioners in this domain. This research proposes a new technique, called Buffered Synchronous Aggregation, that addresses this challenge by utilizing unconstrained gradients on the client devices. This method involves calculating the optimal aggregation point, independent of the learning rate, and then utilizing a buffer to calculate the gradient at this optimal point. This results in a more efficient and effective learning process, especially in scenarios with diverse data distributions across the client devices. Our study demonstrates that this method outperforms the conventional gradient aggregation methods, particularly in scenarios with large data sets, and our implementation shows that it can be an efficient and scalable solution. To achieve multi-language speech recognition using transfer learning, researchers have been exploring methods to share knowledge across languages. Although direct sharing of knowledge has shown promise but also presents difficulties. To overcome these challenges, researchers have proposed several strategies such as weight sharing with distinct offsets for each language, using a language-independent encoder and decoder, and employing a shared embedding layer. Additionally, other methods such as multi-task learning and partial fine-tuning of pre-trained models have also been successful. Through the use of these transfer learning techniques, the need for extensive data collection is reduced, enabling the deployment of speech recognition systems in low-resource language and cross-language settings. Despite the advancements made so far, there are still issues with the loss of sequential characteristic and character-level information due to the use of subword models. To address these limitations, researchers have been experimenting with the use of character-level encoders in addition to subword models. Although these methods have shown some success but also increase the model complexity. To achieve similar results using just one type of encoder, researchers have been comparing the effectiveness of different encoders. For example, the use of a shared embedding layer was compared with other encoder types such as a language-specific RNN encoder and a language-independent transformer encoder. The results of these comparisons were then used to further modify the embedding layer to include additional information similar to the offset-based method. By incorporating the character-level information into the embedding layer, the model complexity was also reduced. The proposed method, known as the shared embedding layer with context, was tested on the 300-hour Librispeech corpus containing data from five languages. The results showed a significant improvement in speech recognition accuracy when the model was trained using the proposed method. For example, the character error rate was 5.4% when recognizing speech from any of the languages, 2.3% when recognizing speech from the same language, and 3.4% when recognizing speech from any of the languages without using character-level information. The use of a shared embedding layer with context allowed the model to share knowledge across languages with just a few thousand parameters, achieving state-of-the-art results in multi-language speech recognition without any additional loss function or model modifications. This study introduces a novel graph dataset called Twitch Players, derived from the online gaming platform Twitch, where users are represented as nodes and social connections as edges. The dataset's unique characteristic lies in its dynamic structure, as nodes continuously appear and disappear over time due to the joining and leaving of users. A unique feature of this dataset is the presence of structural roles within the graph, specifically targeted node subsets that the authors refer to as high-proximity groups. These groups are characterized by users who, despite not being directly connected, share close similarities with each other. The development of a node embedding evaluation metric called PMR is also presented, where the accuracy of node representations is assessed based on their ability to maintain proximity among group members. Through extensive experiments using the Twitch Players dataset, a comparison of various node embedding algorithms, including GAE, GraphSAGE, and ROLX, shows that some algorithms produce node representations that preserve group structure, while others fail to do so. The results indicate that only a subset of the evaluated algorithms meet the desired criteria, demonstrating the practical utility of the PMR metric. The implementation of the ROLX algorithm, which utilizes an optimization technique called constrained gradient penalty, surpasses the baseline GAE method in terms of PMR score but fails to achieve the same level of performance in external node classification tasks due to the influence of the temporal smoothing effect. The study concludes by highlighting the challenges associated with the concurrent occurrence of node and edge dynamics in graph datasets and the potential applications of proximity-preserving node embeddings in social network analysis. The evaluation of node embeddings using the Twitch Players dataset also raises interesting research questions concerning the utilization of temporal node embedding techniques and the development of constrained optimization methods for graph learning. The study's contributions are substantial, given the scarcity of scientific literature focused on temporal graph dynamics and high-proximity groups. The evaluation of the implementation of the ROLX algorithm, combined with the analysis of the results, paves the way for the exploration of novel applications of node embeddings in social network analysis. The evaluation of the implementation of the temporal node embedding technique also highlights the utility of the Twitch Players dataset as a benchmark for testing the performance of graph algorithms. This model includes a range of galaxy components, including a central black hole, a galactic halo, active galactic nucleus, a supermassive black hole, and a multi-object nucleus, which are all used to explain the formation of a spiral galaxy like the Milky Way. A key feature of this model is a quasi-stationary state, where a steady flow of matter from the galaxy's nucleus occurs due to gravitational forces from the halo and the central black hole. As a result, a barycentric frame of reference is established, allowing us to analyze the motion of gas within the galaxy. Our analysis shows that the gas moves in circular orbits around the galactic center due to the gravitational potential created by the galaxy's mass. A key factor in this motion is the ratio of the galaxy's rotational velocity to its radial velocity, also known as the epicyclic velocity. This velocity is maximum at a specific radial distance from the galaxy's center and decreases as one moves towards the edge or the center. The galaxy's orbital velocity is influenced by the gravitational pull of the halo and the central black hole, with a small effect from the active galactic nucleus and the supermassive black hole. As a result, a specific range of radial distances exists where the gravitational pull of these components causes the gas to move in elliptical orbits rather than circular ones. These elliptical orbits can lead to the formation of spiral arms in the galaxy due to a density wave that forms as the gas moves. The gravitational pull of the halo and the central black hole also influence the formation of a bar-shaped structure in the galaxy's nucleus, with a ratio that determines whether a bar or a multi-element nucleus forms. A bar-shaped structure can lead to the creation of spiral arms similar to those in the Milky Way, with a density wave that forms as a result of the orbital velocity of the gas. Our analysis also shows that the galaxy's nucleus rotates in a direction opposite to that of the gas due to a phenomenon known as the "dynamical interaction effect." This research investigates the effects of magnetic fields on galaxy collisions within the scope of cosmological contexts. Our study employs a suite of high-resolution simulations to examine how magnetic fields influence the interactions of gas and stellar disks during galaxy collisions. The proposed model incorporates resistive gravitational contracting of gas within a galaxy's potential field and a simplified dust feedback mechanism. The simulations reveal that strong magnetic fields suppress the downfall of gas into a galaxy's core, thereby preventing gas inflow and the resultant super-Eddington accretion. This effect causes a decrease in jet and luminosity production when compared to model predictions made by a previous study. The non-existence of super-Eddington phases results in no or minimal post-merger phases in our simulations, contrasting with the lasting low-luminosity activity seen in the previous study's results. Additionally, strong magnetic fields lead to the disruption of gas disks by stellar bars forming in the central regions of galaxies, a feature absent in simulations involving minimal magnetic fields. As a result of these changes, the probability of jet and luminosity production in our simulations mirrors the observed statistical distribution of low-luminosity jet sources in the real world. The effects of magnetic fields on reducing the breakdown of galaxy disks and minimizing jet and luminosity production hold significant implications for the interpretation of multi-epoch jet and luminosity data in real galaxies. Furthermore, the findings of this study have implications for the distribution of jet and luminosity probabilities in relation to galaxy mass, suggesting a more intricate relationship than a simple linear correlation. Consequently, any analysis utilizing the results of this study in a theoretical modeling of the relationship between galaxy mass and the probability of jet and luminosity production may require a more complex interpretation, taking into account the influence of magnetic fields, to accurately reflect the true nature of this relationship. Nevertheless, the relationship between galaxy collisions and the resultant production of jets and luminosity is more intricate and subject to a variety of factors, including the probability of collision axis orientation, collision speed, and whether or not the associated black holes have been in a relationship of binary engagement. Therefore, any attempt to utilize the findings of this study in a statistical analysis of real data must consider these additional variables, which will further complicate the analysis and likely result in a large degree of variability, thus necessitating a more substantial sample size for any such analysis. Nevertheless, the fact that the probability of jet and luminosity production in our simulations matches the observed statistical distribution of low-luminosity jet sources in the real world provides a suitable starting point for any such analysis.

Our solution to the 2nd COVID-19 Detection Classification Challenge has been successfully presented at the Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2021, where our team ranked 1st in the open set testing category for classifying X-ray images indicating the severity of COVID-19 infection.  To facilitate accurate diagnosis, we developed an infection-aware classification model using a novel contrastive mixup classification approach.  Initial attempts at applying existing self-supervised learning techniques failed, prompting us to create a custom contrastive mixup classification method that involved a unique strategy for data augmentation, labeled mixing.  By incorporating an infection-aware view for mixing, we successfully expanded the scope of open-set recognition to include not just novel classes, but also new images depicting COVID-19 severity levels.  A key aspect of our strategy involved the use of a contrastive mixup loss function that penalized both classification and augmentation-related inconsistencies.  Furthermore, we employed a robust mixing policy to minimize the impact of mixing on classification accuracy.  The effectiveness of our approach was validated by enhancing the baseline model's performance, achieving an overall accuracy of 73.32% (a 3.32% increase) and an IOU of 0.6522 (a 0.0622 increase) on the COVID19-CLS dataset.  To facilitate reproducibility, our code has been made available on an open-source platform.  Notably, our open-source code has been downloaded over 1000 times and has become the leading repository related to COVID-19 classification on GitHub.  In addition to our competition ranking, our team received the Best Application Award in the Self-Supervised Learning Challenge (S2S-Challenge) held during ICLR 2022.  In accordance with the request of the COVID19-Cls Challenge organizers, our approach has been integrated into a leading COVID-19 classification dataset, namely the COVID19-Cls Challenge dataset, which has been adopted as one of the baseline models for the 3rd COVID19-Cls Challenge held during the IEEE International Conference on Biometrics and Biometric Engineering (ICBBE) 2022.  In order to facilitate continuous evaluation of our solution, our team has been selected as one of the challenge winners for the 3rd COVID19-Cls Challenge.  In addition to our competition ranking, our team received the Best Application Award in the Self-Supervised Learning: From Representation to Valuable Resources (S2S-Challenge) held during ICLR 2023

To overcome this limitation, our proposed model leverages Meta-Learning to achieve successful GERR across multiple domains with minimal adaptation data. Specifically, our model builds on existing sequence-to-sequence foundations by incorporating a continuous cross-domain contrastive loss during few-shot learning. The standard approach of assuming a normal distribution for estimates doesn't account for the fact that they are rounded to the nearest integer, effectively following a distribution that is a combination of two overlapping wedges of a unit sphere. As a result, standard statistical methods are unreliable and tend to underestimate the level of variation in estimates, leading to inaccurate confidence intervals. A new method has been developed to create a reliable framework for estimating totals and constructing confidence intervals when ratings are rounded to the nearest integer. The proposed method uses a specific probability distribution that reflects the effects of rounding and can be applied to estimates that are based on a combination of individual ratings. The new method is compared to the standard approach to show the significant improvement it yields in estimating totals and constructing confidence intervals. The benefits of the new method are illustrated using actual data from two real-world surveys. The method is particularly useful for handling a type of bias known as mid-range estimation bias, which occurs when the rounded averages of diverse groups are compared, and the new method is also used to create a correction factor to minimize this type of error. The proposed method can also be used to compare means that are based on average ratings that are rounded to the nearest integer, and a simulation is conducted to evaluate its performance in a variety of scenarios. The new method proves to be highly accurate and efficient, and it is recommended as the standard approach for estimating totals, constructing confidence intervals, and comparing means in the absence of actual group data. The proposed method can be used in any scenario where mid-range estimation bias needs to be accounted for, and it is particularly useful in survey research, psychology, and any other field that involves collecting data through self-reporting. The new method is simple to implement and is unaffected by the specific characteristics of the individual data points, and it can be used in any scenario where a normal distribution is assumed. The method is robust and reliable, and it can be used in any scenario where a standard statistical method is employed. The proposed method is highly accurate and efficient, and it is the best solution for any problem that involves estimating totals, constructing confidence intervals, or comparing means based on average ratings that are rounded to the nearest integer. Deep learning models excel at classifying images with optimal accuracy, yet their performance significantly declines when applied to unfamiliar image types. This domain-related issue hinders the widespread use and adaptability of deep learning in various applications and limits its ability to efficiently transfer knowledge across different image domains. Current leading approaches in unsupervised domain adaptation techniques involve using a trained conversion model to transform the source and target domains into a shared, familiar domain before adjustment. However, these methods overlook the diverse nature of data within each domain and the complex transformations that cannot be fully accounted for by a single projection. In contrast, our proposed novel framework bypasses the reliance on a conversion model by integrating two key components: one that uses a disentangled latent representation to differentiate the inherent class-related and domain-specific features, and another that employs a resource-sharing filter-sharing strategy to adjust the target domain by minimizing the gap with the source domain. By utilizing a single shared latent representation that captures the features inherent to all classes and the specific characteristics of each domain, our model achieves a more adaptable and efficient adjustment of the target domain. Our results demonstrate significant improvements over the current state-of-the-art methods on the MNIST, SVHN, and VOC-07 datasets, indicating that our novel approach yields more accurate scores with less overfitting. Furthermore, our model's unique architecture enables seamless extension to multi-domain adjustments, facilitating a wide range of real-world applications and a substantial reduction in the required batch size. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/ruotianeng/UDA.git. The pioneering work presented in this paper has paved the way for the further exploration of an unresolved issue in the deep learning community: the unsupervised domain generalization problem. Although our results in the domain adaptation setting outperform the current state-of-the-art methods, the models we tested failed to achieve comparable performance when applied to previously unseen target domains in the domain generalization setting. In order to overcome this challenge, our model has been modified to incorporate an auxiliary class that differentiates the inherent class-related features in a single domain. The modified model has shown potential in solving the unsolved issue of the domain generalization, yet further research is required to fully address this complex problem. This paper introduces a novel form of functional privacy called DP-Sync, which addresses the increasing concern about functional privacy being compromised due to the rapid expansion of cloud computing and big data processing. A key challenge arises when sensitive information, such as update frequencies in databases, is exposed through query functions. To mitigate this risk, our proposed framework utilizes a combination of differential privacy and functional privacy to protect against both privacy breaches and malicious attacks. We demonstrate the feasibility of achieving DP-Sync privacy in outsourced databases and present an efficient differentially private aggregation protocol (DPAP). By leveraging DPAP, both batch and individual updates can be securely supported while maintaining a balance between privacy preservation and system efficiency. A comprehensive performance assessment of our proposed protocol is conducted across various scenarios, indicating that DPAP surpasses the standard baseline performance by a significant margin. Furthermore, DPAP is adaptable to accommodate diverse preference patterns and prioritization settings, ensuring optimal scalability and flexibility in real-world applications. With the integration of DPAP, our proposed framework DP-Sync offers an optimal solution for safeguarding the privacy of update trends in cloud databases against various attacks. The innovative DPAP protocol provides an effective and scalable solution for the challenging problem of designing update-friendly queries in the presence of privacy preservation constraints. The proposed framework DP-Sync can be applied to a wide range of applications and use cases that involve the secure management of update trends in cloud databases and services. into consideration the impact of randomness. The resulting definition, called
"equity of chance," implies that fairness is unaffected by the level of
risk aversion. The definition of equity of chance is analyzed through the lens
of utility-based preferences and reallocation of income as a means of achieving
it. Our primary goal is to examine how income reallocation accomplishes the
aim of fairness, regardless of the method of equating expected outcomes. A key
finding from this approach is the identification of an "inequity of chance"
measure that quantifies the minimum amount of reallocation needed to achieve
equity, independent of the level of risk aversion. This measure has a clear
interpretation: it represents a portion of the total possible reallocation
that can be accomplished through the optimization of utility-based preferences. 
As such, it holds value for any utility function that is consistent with the
definition of equity of chance and is unique in cases where such equity can
be achieved solely by adjusting the variance of returns. A secondary goal of
this study is to explore various aspects of equity of chance, including its
relation to other definitions of fair games, such as the concepts of mean-variance
efficient portfolios and allay risks, as well as the link between equity of
chance and the properties of utility functions. Our analysis highlights the
importance of considering the specific structure of utility functions when
evaluating the fairness of lotteries. Finally, a utility function is proposed
that encapsulates the notion of equity of chance and can be employed in practice.

chance but also is conducive to utility-based analysis. As such, it offers a

By applying this method to variously designed microcavity lasers, we demonstrate that it effectively differentiates their performance. Furthermore, we find that the spatial entropy of these lasers is directly related to their angular entropies, reflecting a common underlying property - the conservation of total entropy. Saturn's northern polar hexagon, formed by strong eastward winds, has been monitored for over a decade by NASA's Cassini spacecraft. Initially observed to be stable despite predictions of vortex breakdown within five years, the anomaly required further exploration. A possible explanation emerged from analyzing Cassini data, revealing that the hexagon's inner 5,000 kilometers fluctuates in temperature in sync with the 30.5-year Saturnian seasonal cycle. As the polar summer approaches, a temperature difference is anticipated between 3-6 Kelvin. If confirmed, this discovery highlights the importance of seasonal atmospheric variations in maintaining the polar vortex strength, a phenomenon also observable in Jupiter. It is predicted that the vortex will break down when the temperature difference reaches 6 Kelvin during the next southern summer. A comparable pattern exists with the GRS (Great Red Spot) on Jupiter, suggesting that atmospheric circulation patterns on these gas giants have a level of resilience to external influences from the planet's core and possible internal heat generation. A potential analogy to these phenomena can be drawn with mid-latitude jets on other exoplanets and brown dwarfs, offering a means to study their atmospheric dynamics. It is also proposed that this mission should also utilize extreme and medium spectral profiling in order to gain a deeper understanding of the atmospheric circulation patterns within the hexagon. Furthermore, the potential discovery of Saturn's ring system "taste", influenced by the interaction between the ring system and the planet's magnetic field, could also be investigated by this mission. Our study uncovers new features of non-equilibrium behavior in quantum double dark-soliton states for one-dimensional repulsive boson gases. We find a specific scaling in the condensate fraction with respect to finite system size, which we utilize to analyze the full time-dependent density profile. We also identify a particular "scaling time" for the quantum double dark-soliton state, where the density still exhibits an intricate time-dependent pattern, yet the behavior of the condensate fraction is fully captured by its equilibrium or non-equilibrium value at this time. We demonstrate that the half-Gaudin model, a strongly interacting system, can be used to analytically derive the time-dependent density matrix of the quantum double dark-soliton state through the second-leg matrix product density matrix transformation. Our findings can be experimentally verified with current trap experiments. We further propose a method for distinguishing between the quantum double dark-soliton state and a coherent state composed of two solitons. Additionally, we provide a theoretical explanation for the observed "breathing mode" behavior in recent 1D boson gas experiments and suggest strategies for testing our results in these systems. DiscSense is a novel method introduced in this research to create a practical and effective testing tool for the word embeddings' fairness in two significant aspects: 1) the examination of the embedded meanings of discourse indicators such as slurs, and 2) the verification of the similarity of the embedded meanings of these indicators across different discourse contexts. Knowledge representation through ontologies is a widely used approach in the knowledge engineering domain, allowing for a structured and symbolic expression of knowledge and its relationships. However, creating or updating ontologies based on text sources, which possess a high information capacity, proves to be a challenging and time-consuming process for both humans and machines. The model further showcases its potential for continuous learning and ontology refinement through subsequent iterations. In machine learning, particularly in model-agnostic techniques like Lasso and Random Forest, the issue of model ambiguity has been extensively explored in the context of overfitting and model selection. However, the field of machine learning and its subset, scientific machine intelligence, also involves interpreting and verifying the results obtained from models that are inherently ambiguous. Consequently, the focus has shifted from simply measuring ambiguity to evaluating the practical implications of model uncertainty on downstream tasks. In this work, we introduce the concept of practical ambiguity and explore its connection to prediction-related ambiguity through case studies in predictive and explanatory contexts. We demonstrate that the current methodology for evaluating ambiguity is limited and often unsuitable for complex datasets, recommending the use of metric-free approaches such as bootstrapping instead of numerical scoring methods. Furthermore, our results indicate that the selection of features should consider both efficiency and effectiveness when implementing simple and complex models in predictive and explanatory contexts respectively. Additionally, our research highlights the benefits of an ensemble-based approach over traditional methods in modeling real-world datasets and highlights the significance of robustness in scientific machine intelligence, achieving a balance between model performance and practical ambiguity. Our findings are illustrated through an open-source code using Python and the MLJToolkit. Leveraging the adage 'extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence,' our work suggests that the evaluation of a machine learning model should be based on multiple robust results rather than a single outcome. Our research provides an open-access framework that encompasses a comprehensive evaluation of a machine learning model comprising several robust results, incorporating a suite of diverse methods, and guarantees the reproducibility and reproceptibility of the findings. This guarantee is enabled by the use of Beaker, a lightweight, shell-based testing framework designed for the evaluation of machine learning methods. This testing framework allows for the inclusion of diverse methods in the evaluation process, a key aspect of studying the variability of results. Our research is a response to the call to prioritize the development of more effective machine learning methods that are robust in their results rather than focusing solely on the advancement of theoretical learning models. Our work is an instance of the former category, as it presents a practical implementation of a robust machine learning method that has achieved results that are comparable to the current state-of-the-art models in the field. Our code is available at https://github.com/ambim/ambim and the testing framework used in this research is available at https://github.com/ambim/mljtk. Our research is also an entry for the 2022 KDD Cup winning solution at https://github.com/ambim

We introduce a novel concept for a shared semantic framework that can be applied across multiple languages, where each language's word representations are organized into distinct clusters that correspond to a unified vocabulary. To achieve this, we develop a new method for supervised word embedding that produces cluster-consistent representations. By leveraging this technique, we create a multilingual word representation system using only a small amount of labeled data. Specifically, we utilized a relatively small set of labeled data to establish relationships between words in one language and then automatically extended these associations to other languages. The results of our approach were evaluated through a variety of tests, including clustering and classification. The findings indicate that our method effectively preserves the inherent structure of each language's semantic landscape. Notably, when applying this technique to multiple languages, the code and models trained on one language can be easily adapted for use with other languages, thus facilitating the creation of a shared semantic framework across many languages. The proposed method also offers a solution to the oov (out-of-vocabulary) issue, where words that do not have pre-trained embeddings can be accurately predicted by our method. Conversational agents between humans can make mistakes by misinterpreting user commands due to uncertain or incomplete labeling of training data. The issue persists even after the agents are trained and are triggered by labeled dialogue data, which is often inaccurate or incomplete. The problem of modeling label uncertainty in training data has not been effectively addressed by current methods, which typically rely on supervised learning techniques. Our proposed framework, ASSIST, aims to enhance the robustness of conversation state estimation by incorporating label uncertainty. By modeling the uncertainty of labeled data as represented by a non-deterministic form, the model is trained using a score-matching objective that takes into account the uncertainty of labels, which is achieved through the reparameterization trick and the score-matching objective function. Our proposed framework also includes an uncertainty-aware loss function to correct flawed labels, which is accomplished by matching the uncertainty of the predicted conversation states with the uncertainty of the labeled data. Unlike conventional regular expressions, these extended patterns permit the use of greedy quantifiers, mutual exclusion operators, and recursive references, which can be seen as a subset of context-sensitive rules. Unlike the approach of translating to automata, our method directly compares the patterns in a more efficient manner, leveraging a set of basic inequalities that can be derived from the rules governing the patterns, somewhat akin to the method for comparing context-free grammars through monoids. This comparison approach is the foundation for solving any variability issue arising from these extended regular expressions, which involves solving a system of inequalities that can be resolved using our established comparison rules. Our research also offers an efficient algorithm for solving inequality issues, and we provide an implementation of this algorithm through a command-line tool and an interactive online sandbox for users to test its effectiveness.
