A proposed new method for creating super-intense laser pulses in the petawatt range involves combining two different techniques: polarization modification of linearly polarized pulses and enhancement through nonlinear interaction with a magnetized plasma. Our research shows that these methods are not only compatible but also complementary, allowing for a significant increase in the peak power of the laser pulses. By modifying the polarization of a multi-petawatt laser pulse from linear to circular through a relatively short length of highly dense plasma, and then passing this pulse through a layer of low-density plasma with a different magnetic field strength, the peak power of the laser can be increased by a factor of up to 30. The optimal performance is achieved when the nonlinear effect and the change in magnetic field are both significant, resulting in an enhancement of the peak power and a increase in the peak intensity by several orders of magnitude. This method is particularly effective for laser pulses with durations between 0.1 and 1 picoseconds. The proposed scheme is especially useful for laser facilities that already have multi-petawatt capabilities and can modulate the polarization of their laser pulses. By incorporating this method, these facilities can achieve the highest peak powers required for certain scientific applications, such as creating high-energy, collinear dual-laser beams in the study of quantum electrodynamics with strong-field effects, without the need for significant upgrades. The proposed method can also be used to increase the peak power of laser pulses in experiments involving the interaction of high-intensity lasers with matter in extreme conditions of strong magnetic fields and high electron accelerations, such as the creation of electron-vacuum undocks, the emission of extreme ultraviolet and soft x-ray radiation, the acceleration of electrons and protons to high energies, and the generation of coherent Thomson radiation in the x-ray and soft x-ray range. Furthermore, this method can enable the creation of two laser pulses with peak powers enhanced to the multi-petawatt range, obtained from a single multi-petawatt pulse with a duration between 0.1 and 1 picosecond, by using a plasma with a specific design and a suitable magnetic field strength. This design allows for the optimization of the peak power of one of the two pulses, while also enhancing the peak power of the other pulse to the multi-petawatt range. Additionally, we show that the proposed method can be used to create two laser pulses with different wavelengths, obtained from a single multi-petawatt pulse with a duration between 0.1 and 1 picosecond

The nature of the tau lepton, taking into account possible contributions from neutrinoless double beta decay and the Karlhuber process, is reassessed within the Standard Model, with a focus on the tau's electric dipole moment. A new restriction on the tau's dipole moment is established in relation to its parent process, and with regard to the Karlhuber process, it is found that the current experimental limit on the tau's dipole moment already contradicts expectations from theory. Furthermore, the implications of a large tau dipole moment on the Karlhuber process are calculated, revealing that future experiments aimed at detecting this process at LHCb and the tau factory CosmIC would be sensitive to the tau's dipole moment at a level where it could be significantly contradicted by the data. Moreover, the approximation used to calculate the tau's dipole strength in the Karlhuber process is identified as insufficient and a more comprehensive calculation is proposed. The resulting logarithmic enhancement of the differential cross-section in the energy range accessible by LHCb and CosmIC, due to the tau's electric dipole strength, is found to be substantial, with a factor of up to 25 for CosmIC's planned beam energies. This insight is crucial for interpreting the outcomes of experiments aimed at discovering the Karlhuber process. Finally, the significance of the tau's electric dipole strength in its parent process, two-body decay, is highlighted, with future opportunities to detect the tau's dipole moment at CosmIC in this context also identified as significant. One type of error that poses significant hurdles is the rank-one error, which arises from various sources including the application of the James-Benn-Bright-Dunskern (JBBD) decoder or the Cholesky decomposition of positive semidefinite operators. In this work, we introduce a new decoding method that uses a symmetric rank matrix to recompress the corrupted operator, allowing for an exact reconstruction of the original operator when the corrupted version is of a lower rank. These lenses, already effective at detecting transient events with large fields of view, can be easily integrated and aligned to cover an even broader area of approximately 1 square degree. This enhancement will allow for the detection of shorter-duration transients and facilitate real-time targeting of sources in real-time, supported by a dedicated telescope control system. This concept, which can be implemented using a 4x4 array of lobster-eye lenses, will enable the simultaneous observation of over a thousand X-ray bright active galactic nuclei while detecting transient events with a rate of $\sim$1 event per second. The rapid spread of COVID19 led various governments to enforce strict lockdowns, resulting in substantial reductions of over 80% in human mobility within 24 hours in multiple major cities. Consequently, the sudden drop in urban interaction rates prompted emergency policy responses, as well as a surge in interest from social scientists, economists, and health experts, who sought to comprehend the underlying factors influencing disease transmission in urban settings. By analyzing location visitation data from 30 million users across five major cities, our findings reveal that a significant increase in people working from home, combined with elevated adherence to social distancing guidelines during the pandemic, resulted in a notable reduction in the overall gap between interaction patterns among the richest and the poorest. However, as lockdown restrictions were eased, the initial positive reduction in the income disparity of urban interactions began to reverse, with the added factor of working from home no longer providing the same beneficial impact once considered essential. As a result, the overall income disparity of urban interactions returned to its pre-pandemic levels. When considering various explanations for these changes, our data analysis suggests that the shift in urban interaction patterns during the pandemic was primarily driven by changes in people's behavior rather than factors such as increased remote work in higher-income households, with the latter actually showing a decline in some cities. Moreover, our research reveals that the rise in home delivery services and enhanced public awareness of keeping distances may have contributed to a more sustained reduction in physical interactions between individuals, with potential long-term implications for mitigating urban epidemics. The dissemination of false news poses a growing threat to both online credibility and real-world consequences. To combat this issue through text analysis, our research focuses on distinguishing true and false articles by analyzing online posts. A key obstacle in tackling this problem is the extensive use of misleading information present in false news articles, which hinders deep learning models from accurately differentiating between true and false information. To address this challenge, we employ an innovative technique called automated text condensation, which compresses an article into a compact summary of crucial phrases. By incorporating this condensed version into the input features, our model achieves enhanced performance compared to the baseline methods, utilizing a BiLSTM classifier with BERT-based embeddings as the primary feature extractor. Furthermore, we discovered that only utilizing the condensed text can effectively identify false news with similar efficiency, indicating that a simple yet effective approach exists. Our work's findings showcase the effectiveness of text condensation in enhancing the performance of deep learning models for the false news classification task. This research investigates how curvature impacts the behavior of random fields defined on Gaussian manifolds. It demonstrates that in the case of Gaussian feature maps, the impact of curvature is precisely quantified by a formula linking the curvature to the rate at which the Riemannian volume within a specific distance decreases as the feature map's intensity increases. This finding holds significant importance in the context of random geometric graphs, Gaussian random fields, and manifolds with low fractional curvature, and is accompanied by accompanying visual demonstrations and analytical proofs in the appendices. Additionally, it identifies an asymptotic regime with potentially curvature-independent properties for Gaussian random fields on manifolds with non-increasing low-order curvature, and a corresponding discussion on random geometric graphs' behavior is also provided. A notable outcome of this investigation is the explicit characterization of the phase transition in random geometric graphs on hyperbolic spaces, a problem previously studied through Monte Carlo simulations but never through analytical methods. A key aspect of this analysis is the utilization of a precise expression that relates the curvature of a specific Riemannian manifold to the nearest neighbor distance in that manifold. This expression can be applied to any Riemannian manifold with a non-positive curvature, and for angular manifolds, it yields a phase transition similar to that observed in graphs constructed on the unit sphere. To compensate, replacing squared losses with absolute differences in the M-estimator can provide resistance to outliers. Nevertheless, estimating parameters in this robust model is complicated by an irreducible curvature in the objective function, which hinders the convergence of PCA-based algorithms. In this paper, we demonstrate a practical and efficient algorithm for computing robust principal components in the presence of rotational symmetry, leveraging an alternative formulation that exploits the symmetry to reduce the dimensionality effectively. The proposed method achieves linear convergence on top of a robust starting point, whereas a preprocessing technique allows us to obtain such a robust starting point efficiently. Our results are further supported by simulations and real-world applications, indicating a notable improvement over PCA in predicting relationships with only a slight decrease in prediction accuracy in clean data sets and a substantial improvement in handling data with contamination. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm compares favorably to existing methods for robust PCA, including both iterative and second-order methods, in terms of both efficiency and accuracy. As a result, our algorithm provides the most efficient and accurate solution for robust PCA in the presence of rotational symmetry to date. Moreover, the proposed algorithm is particularly effective for rotating axes and can be applied to non-rotating axes as well. In the case of non-rotating axes, the algorithm reduces to an iterative hard thresholding method, whereas for rotating axes, the algorithm involves a more complex iteration that includes both a hard thresholding and a rotation step in each iteration. The complexity of this algorithm is quite high, with an iteration complexity of O(n) in each iteration, where $n$ denotes the sample size, making it less suitable for large data sets. Nevertheless, the proposed algorithm can be modified further to use an approximate update for the rotation step, resulting in a more efficient algorithm with an iteration complexity of O(log n) in each iteration. The majority of low-mass binary systems consist of compact objects with unknown spin properties, often referred to as the'missing population.' A subclass of these systems, asynchronous polars, hold potential in identifying these missing objects. Asynchronous polars are a type of binary system characterized by asynchronous orbital and rotational periods. They exhibit unique X-ray spectra that can be analyzed using the RXTE/ASM's toughness ratio ($\log R_{XS}$) to determine their accretion status. By utilizing data from the RXTE/ASM, we investigated the link between the X-ray toughness ratio and the orbital period in asynchronous polars. Our key findings include a distinct $\log R_{XS}$ threshold at $1.32$, below which systems exhibit a positive correlation between $\log R_{XS}$ and the fractional day period, indicating a clear path for identifying asynchronous polars in data sets devoid of coverage. Conversely, systems above the $\log R_{XS}$ threshold of $1.32$ do not exhibit such a correlation, likely due to non-synchronous polars displaying similar spectra. By pinpointing the $\log R_{XS}$ threshold, we were able to identify three additional non-synchronous polars, namely EXO 03319-5254, H 0750-10, and H 0830-0053. These discoveries highlight the effectiveness of utilizing the toughness ratio to differentiate between asynchronous and non-synchronous polars. Moreover, we propose that EXO 03319-5254, exhibiting the highest $\log R_{XS}$ value of all polars, serves as a prime target to study the behavior of non-synchronous polars in detail. Furthermore, we establish that a considerable subset of non-synchronous polars can be distinguished by their optical variability rather than X-ray characteristics alone. Lastly, we emphasize the significance of incorporating the X-ray toughness ratio in future surveys to accurately identify asynchronous and non-synchronous polars. Additionally, we highlight the value of cross-referencing optical variability as an alternate method for discovering these binary systems. This research underlines the importance of examining the relationship between X-ray toughness ratios and spin periods in low-mass binary systems to better comprehend the behavior of accretion and the underlying physics that govern it. Implementing the same numerical techniques for both a unified and a segmented approach, where the Reduced Basis Method is combined with a fixed point strategy and a Newton-Raphson method, allows for a more precise assessment of their relative merits. A chosen test problem, involving the oscillation of a flexible cylinder in a laminar fluid flow, is too complex for a single degree of freedom model. As the frequency of oscillation increases, significant differences in the performance of the two methods become apparent, with the unified approach consistently demonstrating superior efficiency in both CPU time and the number of degrees of freedom. For mobile robots to effectively explore unfamiliar areas with other entities, a high-level overview of their surroundings is crucial. Currently available navigation systems that map environments rely on 2D or 3D geometric representations, but these can become overly complex when incorporating the network of roads. In such situations, a topological map that focuses on connecting areas rather than specific locations might be more suitable. However, these topological maps usually lack the detail needed to direct a forklift through an area by voice commands. To address this issue, a new representation called HiTMap is presented, combining a topological map with a hierarchical structure of text commands for a specific type of industrial vehicle, such as a forklift. HiTMap is particularly useful for navigating tight spaces and directing the vehicle around obstacles through voice commands. To validate HiTMap, a series of experiments were conducted by comparing it to the conventional methods used for industrial vehicles. The results show that HiTMap achieves a more efficient and precise route with lower command risk, especially in tighter spaces. Furthermore, the representation's scalability and flexibility make it adaptable to various environments and vehicles. Despite this setback, the field has seen little development since then. Building on earlier work by Barendsen and Barendsen, we successfully established a more comprehensive version of lambda-cubication, effectively extending the earlier result in a way that addresses the counterexample found by Kawabe. This research introduces an innovative approach called FourierMask, which employs the Fourier transform to enhance implicit neural representations for instance segmentation. Our proposal involves two primary components. Firstly, Fourier feature mapping is applied to implicit functions to facilitate instance segmentation. This is achieved by modifying the feature mapping to utilize the Fourier transform instead, thereby enabling the use of implicit functions to model instance positions and shapes. Secondly, a FourierMask flavour of the BiImplicit neural rendering model is introduced, which models an object's presence or absence using an indicator function. Our model is trained end-to-end using a BiImplicit neural renderer and an indicator function loss, which is derived from a mask auto-encoder. Notably, our approach overlooks the need for bounding box predictions, which is a significant advancement in the field of instance segmentation. Moreover, the Fourier transform allows for flexible modelling of object shapes and instances positions using implicit functions. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through rigorous experiments, which reveal that FourierMask outperforms the current state-of-the-art in the MNIST Linewidth dataset and shows promising results on the Cityscapes dataset, especially when modelling complex scenes and objects shapes. The code for this research has been made available on the GitHub platform. One key limitation of our approach is the requirement for high-resolution images in conjunction with bounding box annotations, which serves as future research direction for this study. Additionally, the simple mask auto-encoder used in this research may not adequately capture intricate instance shapes, which presents another pathway for exploration. Two key implicit function flavours, namely the SphericalHarmonicMask and the FourierMask flavour, emerge as prominent variations of our FourierMask proposal. The former of these flavours is founded upon the spherical harmonic transform, which serves as an alternative to the Fourier transform. Although the spherical harmonic transform flavour exhibits comparable performance to the FourierMask flavour, it encounters difficulties with convergence during training. In contrast, the FourierMask flavour boasts superior convergence properties, which is a crucial advantage. This research further explores two notable implicit function models, namely the BiImplicit neural mask renderer model and the BiImplicit neural occupancy estimator model. Although the BiImplicit neural mask renderer model demonstrates robust performance in modelling instance shapes and positions, it faces difficulties with scaling in high-dimensional settings. In contrast, the BiImplicit neural occupancy estimator model proves more adaptable to such scenarios, which is a key strength. This research culminates with the illustration of an implicit 3D CAD model using both the FourierMask flavour and the spherical harmonic transform flavour. Both of these flavours enable flexible modelling of object shapes and instances

This technique requires highly advanced technology but could potentially offer propulsion efficiencies in the gigawatts range for a minimal propellant cost, which is crucial for effectively exploring deep space. A case study using a chirp laser spectrum is analyzed to demonstrate its feasibility, and the findings show that a relativistic, self-consistent field can be achieved through the combination of a relatively short, high-intensity pulse and a longer, less intense background of low frequency radiation. This achieves optimal results in a narrow window of optimal duration, which demands a high level of control over the laser spectrum. A discussion on potential designs for a propellant-less ion propulsion system based on a very large array of semiconductor diodes is also included. The research combines eye-tracking data with machine learning to distinguish between Palsy and non-Palsy patients.  The proposed method is eye-centered and pupil-based, using minimal information for classification, thereby addressing potential biases in full-face assessments. However, the effectiveness of this approach is validated only once the model is trained on the data provided in the supplied dataset. The concept of generating highly polarized positrons using thin targets illuminated by intense lasers is theoretically sound, but in practice, it is difficult to achieve sufficient polarization levels due to the overwhelming production of unpolarized pairs. To overcome this issue, we propose using a thick target in a state of strong polarization, where the increased density compensates for the lower brightness of the positron beam. In a recent experiment, a 10 terawatt laser beam shone on a centimeter-scale foil target resulted in a 100 micron thick positron layer, highly polarized and extending 1 millimeter into the void. The findings indicate that positrons produced under these conditions have >99.9% likelihood of being polarized in the direction of the target, and that the positron density in the layer can be as high as 10^8 per cubic micron for a certain thickness range. The experiment also revealed that the positron polarization maintains its 1 millimeter thickness, and the layer's density can be modified by adjusting the energy at which the positrons are collected. The results demonstrate the feasibility of producing thick, polarized positron layers, a potential resource for a variety of applications, including proposed initiatives to directly observe the interaction between light and electric and magnetic fields in vacuum. In particular, it may involve the creation of a continuous, polarized electron-positron stream in a storage ring for observation with quantum electrodynamics-based systems. The potential of this technique to significantly influence such experiments is also discussed in the report. By leveraging the variation in threshold voltage with temperature, this inverter-based circuit transforms temperature into a voltage, which is then converted to a binary format via two digital comparators. The inclusion of digital delay lines with different bit weights facilitates the calculation of a weighted average of multiple voltage readings, yielding a more accurate temperature measurement. Long-lived stars maintain equilibrium under thermal, mechanical, and magnetic forces, 
with approximately uniform magnetic fields along their axis, yet these fields can 
change over time as the stars evolve. This study focuses on non-radiative, hydrostatic 
equilibrium in stars and uses linear adiabatic perturbation theory to analyze the 
stability of their magnetic fields under perturbations of any form. The results show 
that in stable equilibrium, the magnetic field is always subject to instability in 
some direction, although in practice, it is stable due to its uniformity and the 
high density of stars. However, in more volatile stars or during critical phases of 
stellar evolution, nonlinear interactions could trigger significant magnetic field 
changes, potentially influencing mass and spin loss processes, wind patterns, and 
the star's overall evolution. This study also highlights the need for dynamic 
simulations that consider magnetic forces and the interplay between internal and 
external processes in stars. This happens particularly when external processes, 
such as mass accretion, impact the star's magnetic field, affecting its stability 
and overall behavior. This understanding is significant for understanding the 
behavior of stars and the generation of pulsar magnetic fields. This research 
was conducted by the late Professor Dikra Karakaya's colleagues in collaboration 
with her, and they are dedicating this work to her memory in recognition of her 
contributions to this field of study.

This study establishes a correspondence to represent geometric configurations on a Lie groupoid or smooth stack, using the language of higher geometric quantization. By leveraging the correspondence, we can map configurations to certain abstract objects called functors that preserve structure. These functors can be seen as a higher version of the classical correspondence between algebraic geometric objects and the representations of the symmetric group in a category. The connection between the higher correspondence and the classical one is the basis for a proof that a specific category related to a stack or Lie groupoid is equivalent to a subcategory of the representations of its symmetries in a higher category of algebraic geometric objects. The proof has implications for the type of functors that can be related to configurations on these sophisticated geometric objects. The article also introduces an order on the set of configurations and uses it to differentiate the higher correspondence from a less complex correspondence. An infrared dark cloud known as the Dragon, located approximately 7.9 kiloparsecs from the Sun, has been the subject of interest recently due to its massive size. Observations using the Hubble Space Telescope have revealed a massive infrared dark filament at its core, extending 52 parsecs in length. By utilizing the Hubble Legacy Archive and a broad range of spectral line data from radio and millimeter wave-lengths, we identified evidence of a gas core contraction within the Dragon, likely a precursor stage for the formation of massive stars. This interpretation is supported by the presence of a highly dense and rotating gas core, as well as an outflow that is still in its early stages, which together indicate that the star formation process within the Dragon is still in its initial phase. Consequently, the Dragon provides a prime target for observing the early stages of massive star formation. Furthermore, it offers a unique opportunity to investigate the process of massive star formation in a large, infrared dark cloud complex.

Therefore, a thorough investigation of the process of massive star formation within the Dragon and similar infrared dark cloud complexes is not only essential to understanding the origin of massive stars, dead stars, and gamma-ray bursts, but also to gaining a deeper understanding of the evolution and formation of galaxies and the universe as a whole.

This is achieved for various settings, including parameters $\theta$ near $\mu$, $\varepsilon$ arbitrarily small, and cases where the underlying process is symmetric or asymmetric. This work builds on prior research for persistent times with slower $n$ dependencies. Additionally, this work implies an asymptotic upper bound for the tail probability of $\tau$ itself, a problem left open in prior research. This work also provides conditions under which the expected time spent above $\theta$ is $\Theta(n^2)$. This result is a foundation for future research aimed at understanding the behavior of higher moments of $\tau$.

While DNA testing is considered the most effective way to diagnose cancer through liquid biopsies, a non-invasive method that has gained popularity in recent years, analyzing nucleus regions within histopathology images can serve as a surrogate approach. However, accurately identifying and segmenting nuclei within these images poses significant challenges due to varying sizes, shapes, and intensities of nuclei and the presence of ambiguous cases such as touching or overlapping nuclei. Existing methods primarily based on single-stage models like Fully Convolutional Networks (FCNs) often struggle to handle these complex situations. In response, we introduce a dual-stage framework, the W-Net, which combines a pre-processing stage using a Region Proposal Network (RPN) to generate potential nucleus regions and a post-processing stage using an FCN to refine these regions. Through extensive testing on the Patch-Label (PL) and Whole-Slide Image (WSI) nucleus datasets, our W-Net model demonstrated superior performance, achieving a Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.793 on the PL dataset and 0.753 on the WSI dataset, which represents significant improvements over the state-of-the-art baseline model. Furthermore, our method exhibits potential applications in cancer grading and classification by correlating nucleus features with cancer progression. Comprehensive evaluations, including visual case studies and comparative analyses with leading baseline models, are also presented to validate the efficacy and versatility of the W-Net. With its high accuracy and flexibility in handling complex nucleus scenarios, our W-Net has the potential to serve as a premier solution for nucleus identification and segmentation within histopathology imaging. Its implementation in cancer diagnosis, particularly grading and classification, is also deemed feasible and worthy of further exploration. The W-Net code has been made publicly available for reference. Nonetheless, the original Patch-Label dataset utilized in the experiments has not been publicly released due to storage constraints and the large size of the dataset, which comprises over 150,000 annotated patches derived from 50 different cancer cases. In response to peer review, we have obtained the approval to share the dataset publicly in order to facilitate further advancements in this domain. The Patch-Label dataset is now made available for download at https://github.com/ghliu89/WSINucleusSegmentation/releases/download/0.1/patch_label_dataset.tar.gz to facilitate further advancements in this domain. In reinforcement learning, achieving optimal policy performance is often hindered by the reliance on external state variables that can complicate problem dynamics. Unfortunately, identifying such variables is difficult due to the inherent complexity of reinforcement learning. This research introduces a novel approach called Variable Elimination Policy (VEP) that automatically discovers and eliminates unnecessary state variables from the learning process. By utilizing a biologically inspired neural network called the Jumping Embedding (JE) policy network, VEP effectively simplifies the underlying state representation, allowing it to learn more efficient and generalized representations of the environment. Through the optimization of a variable-elimination incentive that rewards the reduction of variables, the JE architecture learns to selectively focus on critical state components, thereby enhancing its performance. We demonstrate the efficacy of VEP by applying it to complex, high-dimensional tasks, including the discovery of latent states in navigation scenarios and the elimination of irrelevant sensory inputs in visual control tasks. Our results show that VEP surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art reinforcement learning methods in these tasks. Furthermore, we investigate the ability of VEP to learn flexible and adaptive policies in dynamic environments and highlight the potential applications of variable elimination reinforcement learning in neuroscience and machine learning. Our code is publicly available on https://github.com/ghr96/Variable-Elimination-Policy.

By combining static type checking with refinement types and user-defined properties, the reliability of smart contracts is enhanced, making it more likely for these programs to operate accurately and efficiently in the Tezos blockchain environment. Recent advancements in graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) have led to a surge in applications involving structural data, such as social networks and images with implicit semantics. Despite the effectiveness of these models, a notable absence exists in the current literature - a transparent and intuitive explanation of the learning process in GCNNs. Our work mitigates this gap by providing an analytical expression that breaks down the output of standard graph convolutional layers into their individual component filters, thereby illumininating the relationship between these layers and traditional convolutional neural networks. By leveraging this understanding, we are able to devise an optimized matching algorithm that identifies equivalent GCNN modules across different models, thereby facilitating the transfer of knowledge between them. Our method is particularly useful for both the unsupervised feature learning and the direct application of pre-trained GCNN layers in subsequent classifier layers. We subsequenceley apply this approach to achieve a notable improvement (3.25% accuracy increase) in the benchmarked image classification task, and our feature learning outcomes show a 15% enhancement in the classification accuracy of a subsequent fully connected layer, compared to the current state-of-the-art protocols. Furthermore, our proposed method also demonstrates a notable robustness in the face of noise, thereby extending the applicability of GCNNs to a wider range of applications. Additionally, our approach based on matched filtering provides a unique and compelling justification for the use of the random walk matrix in the graph convolutional layer. Our work also offers an efficient and accurate way to analyze the spectrum of graph convolutional layers, thereby providing a practical solution to the ongoing challenge of layer parameter optimization in GCNNs. Our work is also associated with an interesting historical background, and we are confident that our approach will also be beneficial in identifying the underlying reasons for the success of recent applications involving GCNNs. Additionally, our work is expected to lay the foundation for the development of more transparent and interpretable deep learning models that can efficiently deal with complex structural data. Our approach is particularly relevant to the ongoing quest for the development of efficient and optimized deep learning models that can effectively utilize the implicit semantics present in structural data. Our work is expected to be instrumental in the development of more sophisticated and high-performance GCNN architectures, and our approach is anticipated to have a profound impact on the selection of future optimization strategies for deep learning in the presence of structural data. We've observed a disconnect between computational thinking education and formal verification, with each having its own distinct language and focus. While education emphasizes logic and syntax through pseudocode, often without consideration of soundness, the goal is to foster basic thinking skills in problem-solving. In contrast, formal verification via pseudocode aims for precision and completeness in modeling system behavior. To bridge this divide, we suggest a middle ground where education's rational pseudocode is used in conjunction with explicit variable typing and a limited set of instructional demonstrations. This approach enables students to explore and manipulate rational pseudocode while also teaching the importance of precise modeling in verification. By incorporating this methodology, education and verification can benefit from a shared foundation and a more cohesive approach to teaching algorithms through pseudocode. We've developed a suite of rational pseudocode lessons and demonstrations that can be used with the CodeWorld educational environment in Haskell, and this has shown promise in enhancing both the learning and verification processes. This approach can also be used with other programming languages and education platforms, and we encourage the exploration of this methodology in various teaching and verification contexts. In contrast, other online $k$-means methods we tested, including the Whittle index and a heuristic based on the nearest neighbor, exhibited significantly inferior performance, with the FMUpdate method outperforming them by a factor of at least $5-6$ in our experiments. A key method utilizing deep learning for this enhancement is the use of an unsupervised learning framework called CycleGAN, which produces high-quality images from low-quality data without the need for labeled training data. To address these limitations, we propose a new cycleGAN-based framework called AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN (ASC), which leverages AdaIN modules to separate the learning processes of noise reduction and image restoration. By allowing the unsupervised image restoration component to focus solely on restoring the intensity of CT images, while keeping the noise reduction component flexible to accommodate various low-dose CT images with different noise levels, our method achieves superior results when compared to the state-of-the-art CycleGAN-based methods in four metrics: PSNR, SSIM, NIQE, and PIQE, on both synthetic and real-world data. Moreover, our method's ability to effectively switch between different unsupervised training configurations using the AdaIN module allows it to produce results with a much lower memory consumption and in half the number of iterations compared to the baseline method. In this study, we introduce an exponential delay devaluation model influenced by the Tsallis quantum theory. This model is a modified version of the standard exponential delay devaluation model, widely used in economics to explain consumer behavior under time pressures. The standard model has been criticized for its unrealistic assumptions, including a lack of consideration for uncertainty and risk aversion. In response, we offer a Tsallis-inspired model that incorporates aspects of uncertainty and a milder form of risk aversion, expressed as a non-invariant probability measure. The Tsallis-inspired model reveals that consumers' willingness to pay is enhanced by the patient option when compared to the impulsive counterpart, with an effective decrease that is exponential in nature. This decrease is, however, tempered by the consumer's risk tolerance and a constant that reflects their predisposition towards risk. The model also includes an exponential delay effect, which is modulated by the consumer's time tolerance. The pricing strategy for the patient option is shown to be greater than the impulsive counterpart's price, with the difference following a linear pattern. The model further indicates that the choice between the patient and impulsive options is influenced by the consumer's tolerance for risk and time, with a critical point where the preference switches. The model can also accommodate a wide range of consumer behaviors, including cases where the patient option is preferred, the impulsive option is preferred, or the choice depends on the product in question. The Tsallis-inspired model offers a more nuanced understanding of consumer behavior under time pressures and multiple forms of uncertainty, with implications for firms' pricing strategies and delay devaluation policies. The model suggests that firms should consider offering patient options, with prices calculated using the model's parameters, to maximize sales and revenue in markets subject to uncertainty and risk aversion. The model's findings are validated using real-world data from a supermarket's sales of perishable products. The data show that the patient option is preferred when the delay period is long, the impulsive option is preferred when the delay period is short, and the choice depends on the product when the delay period is medium-length. The data also indicate that the patient option's price is higher than the impulsive option's price when the delay period is long, the impulsive option's price is higher than the patient option's price when the delay period is short, and the prices are equal when the delay period is medium-length. The model can be applied across various markets and industries, with the potential to inform firms' pricing and delay devaluation policies, contributing to better decision-making and improved performance

The notion of negative absolute temperature, initially met with skepticism, has been consistently supported by theoretical models and a substantial number of experimental results. In this presentation, we will begin by explaining the conceptual framework of negative absolute temperature, including a discussion on the Bianchi identity that some argue is the true temperature definition. We then move on to examining the various methods for achieving negative absolute temperatures, whether through optical techniques, atomic and molecular setups, or even macroscopic devices, and discuss the inherent relationships between them. Furthermore, we investigate the fundamental applications of negative absolute temperatures in both thermal and non-thermal equilibrium scenarios, and explore the broader implications for our understanding of temperature and its connections to other physical concepts. Finally, we offer a glimpse into the exciting possibilities that the study of negative absolute temperatures may unlock in the future. Editors: S. Manchanda, A. M. Ignat'ev. Organizers: S. Manchanda, A. M. Ignat'ev. Chair: A. M. Ignat'ev. A significant barrier in developing effective artificial intelligence-based diagnostic systems is the scarcity of high-quality, annotated histological image datasets. This dataset comprises 15,000 images divided into 4000 validation images, 4000 test images, and a remainder of 8000 training images. Each image is tagged with classification information (normal, hyperplastic, adenoma, serrated adenoma/polyp) as well as grading data (low, medium, high) to accommodate the UniTo task definition. To facilitate further advancements in this area, we've also introduced multiple variants of UniToPatho, including a classification-focused subset and a pair of enlarged versions of the primary dataset. Using an inhomogeneous method, we derive exact formulas for structure factors in three higher-spin XXZ models, including the $sl_2$ XXZ chain, the $sl_2$ XXZ ladder, and the $osp_3$ XXZ chain. These formulas demonstrate how single-particle excitations behave within these systems. The obtained results confirm the expected affine quantum-group symmetry as predicted by the Bethe ansatz. Specifically, our findings show that spin-observables follow the rules dictated by this symmetry. Leveraging the structure factors, we calculate various one-particle observables, including the magnetization, specific heat, and double magnetization. These results reveal distinct patterns, including some resembling those found in integrable systems with a higher-spin XXZ point. Moreover, our derivation employs the inhomogeneous Bethe-ansatz approach, utilizing both the diagonal and diagonal-invariant subalgebras of the $sl_2$ quantum algebra. This method enables straightforward extraction of the structure factors from the residues of the scattering matrices. This clear relationship between structure factors and scattering amplitudes significantly simplifies the understanding of one-particle properties in these integrable systems. It also enables the direct verification of the affine quantum-group symmetry through the specific constraints imposed on the scattering matrices. We've derived a formula for the relative quantum homology in a transformed space and analyzed its relationship to the original homology. Furthermore, we've identified conditions under which the transformation maintains the property of extended Lagrangian universality. Additionally, our findings provide insights into the behavior of the Landau-Ginzburg model across different bases. Using deep learning on images can be an effective way to detect diseases, specifically cardiovascular diseases, by analyzing chest X-rays. However, accessing high-quality medical images labeled with cardiovascular disease diagnoses can be challenging due to data privacy restrictions and the need for primary expert diagnoses. Instead of relying on secondary diagnoses from radiology reports, which can be time-consuming and inconsistent, we propose a different approach. By training a deep learning model on edited chest X-ray images along with their associated radiology reports, we can utilize the existing dataset while also protecting patient confidentiality. The model learns to detect diseases directly from the images and uses the edits to ensure the models are illness-aware, reducing the risk of overfitting on report-based features rather than visual signs of diseases. By testing our deep learning framework on the CheXpert dataset, we found that a pre-trained DenseASPP model achieved high accuracy in detecting five specific cardiovascular disease diagnoses when trained with edited images. Moreover, the results showed that the highest performing models were those trained with edited images that aligned with the radiology reports, demonstrating the effectiveness of our illness-aware image modification approach. The modified dataset and associated code are available for use and adaptation by other researchers. The changes made to the images are reversible and do not add any new identifying information, further ensuring patient confidentiality is maintained. The existing dataset can be used as is, without the need for further data collection or primary expert diagnoses. The code and the modified dataset can be found at the following link https://github.com/seyedmohammadghasemi/illness-aware-image-modification, where the pre-trained models can be found in the models folder. The CheXpert dataset used in this study can be downloaded from https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.04043, where the original paper was published in the conference, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 31: Automatic Machine Learning Track, 2023.
